source: PCS v4.0, Para 1.2 (Primacy of Law)
question: A consulting actuary advising an Indian life insurer is instructed by company management to adopt an internal corporate valuation guideline that directly conflicts with a legally binding IRDAI circular. Under PCS v4.0 Para 1.2, how must the actuary proceed?
options: The actuary must seek formal written dispensation from the President of the Institute before complying with the statutory circular.
The actuary may choose either standard at their discretion, provided the choice is prominently disclosed in a footnote to the valuation report.
The actuary must follow the internal corporate guideline because an actuary's primary legal duty of loyalty is to their paying employer.
The actuary must comply with the IRDAI circular, because statutory legislation and judicial legal requirements strictly override professional guidance notes and employer instructions.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Para 1.2, professional guidance is not intended to require members to act in breach of law. Where professional guidance or employer instructions conflict with statutory or judicial legal requirements, the requirements of law strictly prevail.
explanationIncorrect: Option B is wrong because employer loyalty cannot justify violating the law. Option C is wrong because Council dispensation under Para 1.6 cannot exempt a member from statutory law. Option D is wrong because compliance with law is non-discretionary.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 1.1 & 1.3 (Universal Scope)
question: Which of the following correctly describes the scope of application of the Professional Conduct Standards (PCS v4.0)?
options: The PCS applies only to actuaries practicing within India; Indian actuaries working abroad are governed exclusively by local foreign law.
The PCS applies only to Appointed Actuaries and signing consulting actuaries; corporate actuarial employees are exempt.
The PCS applies strictly to Fellows holding a Certificate of Practice (COP); students and associates without a COP are exempt.
The PCS applies unconditionally to all classes of members of the IAI—Fellows, Associates, Students, and Affiliates—whether practicing in India or abroad, and whether employed, consulting, or retired.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Para 1.1, the PCS applies to all members of the Institute of Actuaries of India regardless of membership class (Fellows, Associates, Students, Affiliates), practice area, employment status, or geographical location.
explanationIncorrect: Options B, C, and D are common exam misconceptions. The PCS is universal across all membership grades, employment arrangements, and jurisdictions.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 1.6 (Council Dispensation)
question: Under what conditions may an actuary be granted dispensation from complying with a specific provision of the Professional Conduct Standards (PCS v4.0)?
options: Upon verbal approval from the Appointed Actuary of the insurer being advised.
Upon submitting a unilateral disclaimer in the actuarial valuation report.
Only in exceptional circumstances, upon formal written application to the Council, and granted strictly in writing by the Council of the Institute.
Automatically, if following the provision would result in commercial loss or breach of a private client contract.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Para 1.6, dispensation from compliance with any provision of the PCS can only be granted by the Council in exceptional circumstances, upon formal written application, and must be evidenced in writing.
explanationIncorrect: Neither employer consent, client disclaimers, nor Appointed Actuary approval can dispense with PCS obligations; only the statutory Council has this power.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 2.1 (Integrity & Substance over Form)
question: An actuary calibrating liability reserves for an insurer discovers that applying the minimum regulatory mathematical formula produces a reserve that is clearly inadequate to meet expected future policyholder claims. How does PCS v4.0 govern the actuary's duty?
options: The actuary must report the minimum regulatory figure to the regulator and maintain a private set of internal accounts for the Board.

The actuary must prioritize substance over form and ensure the reserves are genuinely sufficient, as mechanically following a minimum regulatory formula while knowing it produces inadequate reserves breaches professional integrity.
The actuary is legally immune from criticism as long as the mathematical calculation complies with the minimum regulatory formula.
The actuary should adopt the inadequate reserve but reduce their professional fees to compensate the insurer.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Para 2.1, actuaries must uphold professional integrity and prioritize substance over form. Complying with the letter of a regulatory formula while ignoring known adverse realities constitutes professional misconduct.
explanationIncorrect: Option B inverts the principle of substance over form. Option C proposes misleading regulatory disclosures, which is severe misconduct. Option D does not cure reserve insufficiency.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 2.1 (Professional Competence & Due Care)
question: A Fellow with 15 years of exclusive expertise in life insurance valuation is requested by a client to certify a complex marine reinsurance catastrophic excess-of-loss pricing model. The actuary has never worked in non-life reinsurance. Under PCS v4.0 Para 2.1, how must the actuary proceed?
options: The actuary must decline the assignment, or only accept it if they collaborate with an experienced general insurance actuary and disclose this arrangement to the client.
The actuary may accept if they charge a discounted fee to reflect their lack of experience.
The actuary may accept the assignment alone because holding a Fellowship (FIAI) legally certifies universal competence across all actuarial fields.
The actuary should accept the work and rely completely on automated commercial catastrophe software without independent review.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Para 2.1, actuaries must only accept work that is within their professional competence. If specialized knowledge is lacking, the actuary must either obtain appropriate support from a qualified specialist with client consent, or decline the appointment.
explanationIncorrect: Fellowship denotes professional qualification, not omnicompetence across all specialized domains. Software outputs must be validated by competent professional judgment.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 3.1 & 3.2 (Confidentiality & Statutory Compulsion)
question: The Enforcement Directorate (ED), exercising powers of a Civil Court under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), serves a formal statutory summon directing an actuary to provide client cash-flow projections. The client strictly instructs the actuary not to disclose any records. What must the actuary do?
options: Comply with the statutory summon and disclose the required records, as statutory or judicial legal compulsion is an explicit exception to confidentiality under Para 3.2.
Resign immediately from the client engagement to avoid having to comply with either the client or the ED.
Disclose only fabricated or redacted models to protect client trade secrets.
Refuse disclosure to the statutory authority until the client gives express written consent.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Para 3.2, client confidentiality is subject to three strict exceptions, the first being statutory or judicial compulsion by a court or authority possessing competent legal powers. Client consent is not required.
explanationIncorrect: Option B incorrectly subordinates the law to client instructions. Resignation (Option C) does not extinguish a valid statutory summons. Fabricating data (Option D) is a criminal offense.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 3.2 (Public Interest Whistleblowing)
question: During a statutory valuation, an actuary discovers incontrovertible evidence that company directors are actively siphoning policyholder funds, creating a catastrophic insolvency risk. Management refuses to rectify the matter. Under PCS v4.0 Para 3.2, what is the mandatory procedural step before the actuary discloses this to the regulator without client consent?
options: The actuary cannot disclose under any circumstances, because client confidentiality is absolute and permanent.
The actuary may disclose immediately to the press and social media without taking legal counsel.
The actuary must obtain written permission from the company's Board Audit Committee.
The actuary must seek independent legal advice to verify that the public interest disclosure is legally protected and justified before disclosing without client consent.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Para 3.2, public interest whistleblowing to prevent serious crime, fraud, or grave public harm is permissible, but the actuary is mandatorily advised to obtain independent legal counsel prior to disclosure to verify statutory protection.
explanationIncorrect: Disclosing to the press (Option B) violates professional confidentiality. Board permission (Option C) is unachievable in management fraud. Confidentiality is not absolute (Option D).

source: PCS v4.0, Para 3.2 (Confidentiality Exception: Self-Defense)
question: A former client files a formal complaint with the IAI Disciplinary Directorate alleging that an actuary committed gross professional negligence in valuing pension obligations. To defend against the charge, the actuary must disclose confidential scheme asset registers and internal client emails. Is this disclosure permissible under PCS v4.0?
options: No, client confidentiality continues indefinitely and can never be breached, even to defend against professional misconduct charges.
Yes, but only if the actuary pays an arbitration penalty of Rs. 25,000 to the Institute.
Yes, disclosing confidential client information is permitted to the extent reasonably necessary to defend oneself against a formal lawsuit or official disciplinary proceeding.
Yes, but only if the complainant client grants prior written consent to using their files.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Para 3.2, the third recognized exception to client confidentiality is self-defense: members may disclose confidential material strictly to the extent necessary to defend themselves against formal disciplinary charges or legal claims.
explanationIncorrect: Client consent is not required when defending against charges brought by that very client. Fictitious arbitration penalties (Option C) do not exist.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 3.1 (Duration of Confidentiality Duty)
question: An actuary resigns as Appointed Actuary of an insurance company after 7 years of service. Three years after resignation, an investment analyst asks the actuary for confidential historical loss-ratio data from the former employer. How does PCS v4.0 govern this request?
options: The actuary may disclose the information once the insurer publishes its annual audited accounts.
The actuary may disclose the data provided they do not receive financial payment for the information.
The duty of confidentiality expires exactly 1 year after the termination of employment.
The duty of confidentiality continues indefinitely, even after the professional relationship or employment has terminated, unless an exception under Para 3.2 applies.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Para 3.1, the duty of confidentiality is permanent and continues indefinitely even after the member has ceased to act for or be employed by the client.
explanationIncorrect: Confidentiality does not have a 1-year sunset clause, nor does non-payment or subsequent general public accounts extinguish unpublished confidential background data.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 4.1 & 4.2 (Conflict of Interest Protocol)
question: An actuarial consulting firm is approached by Company B (the bidder in a hostile takeover) to value the target company, Company T. The firm already serves as the Appointed Actuary and statutory valuation advisor to Company T. What is the mandatory professional course of action under PCS v4.0 Para 4?
options: The firm may freely accept the assignment from Company B without informing Company T, provided different junior analysts work on the spreadsheets.
The firm must resign immediately from Company T before talking to Company B.

The firm must identify the actual and perceived conflict of interest, disclose it fully in writing to both Company B and Company T, and may only proceed if both parties grant explicit informed consent with robust structural safeguards (Chinese walls).
The firm must accept Company B's offer immediately because competition law encourages consultants to serve multiple industry competitors.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Para 4, the mandatory 3-step conflict protocol requires: proactive identification, full written disclosure to all affected parties, and explicit informed consent. If consent cannot be obtained or safeguards cannot preserve objectivity, the engagement must be declined.
explanationIncorrect: Failing to disclose conflicts (Option B) is severe misconduct under the Second Schedule. Competition law (Option C) does not override ethical conflict rules.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 4.4 (Chinese Walls & Structural Safeguards)
question: Where two competing corporate clients grant informed consent for an actuarial consultancy to advise both on a joint venture, what structural measures must the firm establish under PCS v4.0?
options: The firm must double its consulting billing rate to reflect the added ethical risk.
A verbal agreement among team members not to discuss client work in public cafeterias.
The assignment must be handled entirely by an uncredentialed student trainee without partner oversight.
Physical and electronic information barriers (Chinese walls), separate engagement teams, independent peer reviewers, and strict data partitioning.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Para 4.4, when managing conflicts with informed consent, firms must institute robust, verifiable safeguards including Chinese walls, dedicated segregated personnel, distinct servers/passwords, and independent review.
explanationIncorrect: Informal verbal pacts (Option B) are legally insufficient. Omitting partner oversight (Option C) violates competence rules. Rate hikes (Option D) are irrelevant.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 7.1 & 7.2 (Change of Actuarial Advisor - Client Autonomy)
question: An insurance client informs its existing consulting actuary (Actuary X) that it has decided to terminate their contract and appoint Actuary Y. Actuary X refuses to accept the termination and threatens to withhold historical valuation data. How does PCS v4.0 evaluate Actuary X's position?
options: Actuary X is legally entitled to block the appointment until the client renews the contract for at least one more valuation cycle.
Actuary X is acting in breach of PCS; clients have an unrestricted right to choose and change their professional advisors, and the incumbent actuary must make no attempt to obstruct the transition.
Actuary X may block the successor actuary if Actuary Y has fewer years of post-qualification experience.
Actuary X can withhold statutory valuation files indefinitely if there is an ongoing commercial dispute over unpaid consulting fees.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Para 7.1 and 7.4, client autonomy is fundamental: clients have an absolute right to choose and replace their advisors. The incumbent actuary must not obstruct the transition and cannot use client data as leverage in commercial fee disputes.
explanationIncorrect: Unpaid fees are a commercial debt to be pursued through civil courts, not a professional justification to withhold statutory data or block client handover.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 7.2 & 7.4 (The 10-Day Handover Rule)
question: Actuary A is approached by a corporate client to take over the annual employee gratuity valuation previously handled by Actuary B. Actuary A writes to Actuary B requesting professional clearance. Under PCS v4.0 Para 7.4, within what timeframe must Actuary B respond?
options: Actuary B has 21 days, matching the pleading timetable of the Disciplinary Directorate.
Actuary B is not required to respond unless the corporate client pays an official transition fee.
Actuary B has 30 working days to respond under standard commercial practice.
Actuary B must reply in writing as soon as possible, but no later than 10 calendar days from receipt of the communication.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Para 7.4, the incumbent actuary must provide the required professional handover information as soon as possible, and no later than 10 days from receipt of the inquiry.
explanationIncorrect: The 10-day rule is a strict professional obligation. Failing to reply within 10 days without valid justification constitutes professional misconduct under the First Schedule.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 7.3 (Mandatory Refusal if Client Withholds Consent)
question: A prospective client approaches Actuary P to perform a statutory liability valuation, replacing the incumbent actuary. When Actuary P informs the client that professional standards require writing to the incumbent actuary to inquire about professional reasons, the client adamantly refuses permission, citing confidential commercial fallout. What MUST Actuary P do under PCS v4.0 Para 7.3?
options: Actuary P may accept the appointment provided the client signs an indemnity bond protecting Actuary P against future claims.
Actuary P MUST decline the appointment unconditionally.
Actuary P may proceed with the valuation as long as a prominent disclaimer stating 'No contact with prior actuary' is included in the report.
Actuary P should accept the engagement and secretly send a copy of the final report to the IAI President.
explanationCorrect: PCS v4.0 Para 7.3 is strict, unequivocal, and unconditional: 'If the client refuses permission to contact the incumbent actuary, the newly approached actuary MUST decline the appointment.' There are no exceptions, disclaimers, or indemnity carve-outs.
explanationIncorrect: Proceeding without contacting the incumbent actuary after client refusal is a cardinal ethical violation under PCS v4.0.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 7.4 (Professional Reasons vs Fee Disputes)
question: When an incumbent actuary replies to a successor actuary's 10-day inquiry letter under Para 7.4, which of the following represents a valid 'professional reason' that should be disclosed?
options: The client repeatedly coerced the incumbent actuary to understate claim reserves and threatened termination when the actuary insisted on prudent assumptions.
The client has an outstanding balance of unpaid consulting fees from the previous quarter.
The client is shifting to a consulting firm that quoted lower hourly rates.
The client's Chief Risk Officer is personally disagreeable to work with.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Para 7.4, professional reasons concern matters of integrity, regulatory compliance, coercion, or unethical practices that could impact the successor's decision to accept the appointment.
explanationIncorrect: Commercial fee disputes, fee undercutting, and personal friction are commercial or interpersonal matters, not professional grounds that impede appointment.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 5.2 (Duty to Self-Report Professional Breaches)
question: An actuary discovers that an actuarial report certified two years ago contained a catastrophic mathematical formula error that resulted in material underfunding of a pension trust. The error cannot be rectified without public disclosure. What is the actuary's duty under PCS v4.0 Para 5.2?
options: The actuary is only required to report the breach if a third party files a formal police complaint.
The actuary should destroy the original working models and blame the software vendor.
The actuary should remain silent because the three-year commercial statute of limitations has not yet expired.
The actuary must immediately self-report the unrectifiable material professional breach in writing to the IAI, and inform affected stakeholders.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Para 5.2, an actuary who realizes they have committed an unrectifiable material professional breach has an affirmative mandatory duty to self-report the matter to the Institute promptly.
explanationIncorrect: Concealing known material errors or destroying records compounds the violation into gross professional misconduct under the Second Schedule.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 5.3 & 5.4 (Peer Misconduct Protocol)
question: Actuary M discovers that Actuary N (a peer consultant) has issued an insurance pricing certificate based on deliberately fabricated claim settlement ratios. What is the correct initial course of action for Actuary M under PCS v4.0 Para 5.3?
options: Actuary M must immediately publish an open warning letter on social media naming Actuary N.

Actuary M should first discuss the matter directly with Actuary N to seek clarification and explore rectification, unless doing so would be inappropriate, prejudice client confidentiality, or involve serious fraud; if unresolved or involving serious fraud, report promptly to the Director (Discipline).
Actuary M must contact Actuary N's employer and demand that Actuary N be dismissed immediately.
Actuary M must remain silent because actuaries have no duty regarding peer conduct.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Para 5.3, the peer misconduct protocol requires informal direct discussion first where appropriate to allow clarification or rectification; if serious fraud is involved or the peer refuses rectification, a formal complaint must be lodged with the Director (Discipline).
explanationIncorrect: Public shaming (Option B) violates publicity and confidentiality rules. Remaining silent on known fraud (Option C) breaches collective professional integrity.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 5.5 (Cross-Border Disciplinary Reporting)
question: An Indian Fellow (FIAI) who also holds fellowship in an overseas actuarial body (IFoA) is formally reprimanded and fined by the IFoA for negligence in UK pension calculations. Under PCS v4.0 Para 5.5, what is the member's obligation to the IAI?
options: The member has no obligation to inform IAI because the misconduct occurred outside Indian territorial jurisdiction.
The member must report the overseas disciplinary finding in writing to the IAI Council within 30 days of the order.
The member only needs to report if the fine exceeds GBP 50,000.
The member must surrender their Indian fellowship permanently within 24 hours.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Para 5.5 (Cross-Border Reciprocity), any member subjected to disciplinary sanctions, fines, or suspensions by an overseas professional body or financial regulator must notify the IAI Council in writing within 30 days.
explanationIncorrect: Jurisdictional boundaries do not shield members from ethical reporting obligations to their home institute.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 6.1 & 6.2 (Written Terms of Reference)
question: Before commencing an actuarial valuation engagement for a new client, what must an actuary ensure under PCS v4.0 Section 6?
options: A verbal understanding with the client's finance manager is reached via phone.
The client pays 100% of the estimated professional fees into an escrow account.
The engagement terms are registered with the local Registrar of Companies.
Written terms of reference are agreed upon with the client, defining the scope, deliverables, intended users, access to data, and basis of remuneration.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Para 6.1, members must ensure that the scope of the assignment, the intended users, constraints, and the basis of remuneration are clearly established in writing in the Terms of Reference before beginning work.
explanationIncorrect: Verbal agreements (Option D) lead to scope ambiguity and ethical disputes. 100% escrow deposits (Option B) and ROC registration (Option C) are not statutory professional requirements.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 6.7 (Contingency & Success Fees)
question: An insurer offers an actuary a consulting contract to determine statutory solvency reserves where the fee is agreed as: 'A base fee of Rs. 5 Lakhs, plus a bonus of Rs. 10 Lakhs if the calculated solvency margin exceeds 180%'. How is this arrangement evaluated under PCS v4.0 Para 6.7?
options: It is permissible provided the Board Audit Committee signs a waiver acknowledging the bonus structure.

It is strictly prohibited; contingency or success fee arrangements that compromise an actuary's objectivity or create financial incentives to bias statutory reserving or solvency certifications are unethical.
It is permissible as long as the bonus percentage does not exceed 50% of the total fee.
It is fully acceptable as standard commercial performance-based remuneration.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Para 6.7, fee arrangements contingent on the outcome or results of actuarial calculations are strictly forbidden where they threaten objectivity in statutory reserving, solvency reporting, or financial certifications.
explanationIncorrect: Contingency fees on regulatory reserves create an irreconcilable conflict of interest between commercial greed and policyholder security.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 6.8 & First Schedule (Referral Commissions & Fee-Splitting)
question: An insurance marketing agent offers to refer all corporate gratuity valuation clients to an actuarial firm, on the condition that the actuary pays the agent a 20% referral commission on all client fees collected. How does the ethical framework govern this proposal?
options: It is strictly prohibited professional misconduct; sharing fees or paying referral commissions to non-members for procuring actuarial engagements violates the First Schedule of the Actuaries Act and PCS v4.0.
It is permissible provided the 20% commission is deducted from gross revenues before tax.
It is acceptable if the corporate clients sign an acknowledgement acknowledging the referral commission.
It is legal as long as the marketing agent is licensed as an insurance broker by IRDAI.
explanationCorrect: Under the First Schedule, Part I, Clause 2 & 3 of the Actuaries Act 2006 and PCS v4.0, paying referral commissions, finder's fees, or splitting professional fees with non-members is strictly prohibited misconduct.
explanationIncorrect: Client disclosures or broker licenses cannot legalize prohibited fee-splitting under statutory actuarial legislation.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 8.1 - 8.4 (Advertising & Professional Publicity)
question: An actuarial firm launches an advertising campaign in national newspapers claiming: 'We guarantee 30% lower reserve liabilities than any other actuarial consulting firm in India.' Under PCS v4.0 Section 8, how is this publicity classified?
options: It is acceptable provided the firm has actually delivered lower reserves for at least three past clients.

It constitutes professional misconduct; publicity must be truthful, factual, and dignified, and must not disparage competitors, make unsubstantiated claims, or promise predetermined mathematical outcomes.
It is permissible as long as the advertisement clearly displays the firm's registration number.
It is permissible commercial marketing under the Consumer Protection Act.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Section 8 and the First Schedule of the Actuaries Act 2006, advertising must be informative, objective, and dignified. Promising lower reserves or disparaging peer firms is strictly prohibited touting and misconduct.
explanationIncorrect: Guaranteed lower reserves imply compromised technical standards and violate the fundamental principle of professional objectivity.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 8.4 (Social Media Conduct & Public Commentary)
question: An actuary writes a viral post on LinkedIn alleging that the Appointed Actuary of a prominent insurer intentionally certified fraudulent liabilities in an active, ongoing regulatory investigation. How does PCS v4.0 govern such public statements?
options: Actuaries must refrain from making public or social media statements that disparage peers, prejudge ongoing sub judice or regulatory matters, or bring the actuarial profession into disrepute.
The post is permissible if it receives more than 5,000 likes from insurance industry professionals.
Actuaries have an absolute constitutional right to free speech on social media that overrides Institute conduct rules.
The post is acceptable provided the actuary includes a standard disclaimer stating 'Views are personal'.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Para 8.4 and Council Social Media Guidelines, public commentary that attacks peers, discusses sub judice inquiries, or tarnishes professional standing constitutes professional misconduct.
explanationIncorrect: Disclaimers like 'views are personal' do not insulate members from ethical accountability for public disparagement.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 2.2 (Clear Communication & Jargon)
question: When issuing an actuarial report intended for a non-actuarial Board of Directors, what is the actuary's duty regarding technical terminology under PCS v4.0 Para 2.2?
options: The actuary must omit all references to uncertainty to avoid causing panic among company directors.
The actuary should maximize complex stochastic formulas to demonstrate mathematical superiority to the Board.

The actuary must present the results in clear, intelligible language, explaining the methodology, material assumptions, uncertainties, and practical implications so that intended users can make informed decisions.
The actuary is prohibited from explaining assumptions to non-actuaries to protect intellectual property.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Para 2.2, actuaries must communicate with clarity and transparency, translating technical concepts into actionable, understandable advice for intended users.
explanationIncorrect: Concealing uncertainty or using deliberate obscurantism breaches the fundamental duty of care.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 5.1 (Ignorance Defense Prohibition)
question: In a formal disciplinary proceeding, a newly qualified Fellow pleads that they were unaware of the 10-day handover rule under Para 7.4 because they had not read PCS v4.0 since passing their exams. How is this defense treated under PCS v4.0 Para 5.1?
options: The Disciplinary Committee must dismiss the charges and mandate a 2-hour refresher seminar instead.
Ignorance is accepted as a complete defense if the member has been qualified for less than three years.
Ignorance of the PCS, the Actuaries Act, or Actuarial Practice Standards can never be pleaded as a defense or mitigating factor in disciplinary proceedings.
Ignorance converts Second Schedule misconduct into a minor First Schedule reprimand automatically.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Para 5.1, every member is strictly presumed to know and understand the conduct standards. The plea of ignorance of professional rules is completely barred.
explanationIncorrect: Professional self-regulation requires members to maintain currency with their ethical obligations at all times.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 2.1 (Gifts, Hospitality & Inducements)
question: An actuarial software vendor bidding for a multi-crore valuation software contract with an insurer invites the Appointed Actuary and their family on an all-expenses-paid luxury holiday to Switzerland. How does PCS v4.0 govern the acceptance of such hospitality?
options: The actuary must decline the holiday, because accepting lavish gifts or hospitality that could be perceived as compromising objectivity and professional independence breaches Para 2.1.
The actuary may accept if the software vendor guarantees that their software has zero bugs.
The actuary may accept provided they travel during approved annual leave.
The actuary may accept provided they disclose the holiday in their personal income tax return.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Para 2.1, members must preserve objectivity and avoid accepting gifts, hospitality, or inducements that could reasonably be seen by an objective observer as compromising their professional judgment.
explanationIncorrect: Tax disclosures or personal leave do not sanitize a clear conflict of interest and threat to professional independence.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 2.1 (Delegation & Supervision)
question: A senior consulting actuary delegates complex stochastic liability calculations to a junior trainee and signs the statutory report without reviewing the trainee's formulas or validating the outputs. An error of Rs. 50 Crores is later discovered. Who is liable under PCS v4.0?
options: The senior actuary retains ultimate personal responsibility for all work issued under their name, and is guilty of professional misconduct for failing to adequately supervise and review delegated work.
Only the junior trainee is liable because they physically entered the incorrect spreadsheet formulas.
Only the software vendor who created the spreadsheet application is liable.
Neither is liable because corporate delegation legally transfers all professional liability away from the actuary.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Para 2.1, an actuary who delegates work must ensure adequate supervision and validation; delegation does NOT abrogate or transfer the actuary's ultimate personal professional responsibility.
explanationIncorrect: Actuaries cannot hide behind subordinates; signing a professional report certifies personal responsibility for its technical integrity.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 2.3 (Courtesy & Professional Respect)
question: In a peer review report submitted to an insurer's Board, Actuary K describes the work of predecessor Actuary L as 'the amateurish scribbles of an incompetent fraudster'. How does PCS v4.0 evaluate Actuary K's conduct?
options: Actuary K has committed professional misconduct; members must show courtesy, fairness, and professional respect toward colleagues, expressing disagreements objectively and professionally without derogatory personal attacks.
Actuary K is protected because peer reviewers have absolute legal immunity to use any language they wish.
Actuary K's language is permissible as long as the peer review report is marked 'Strictly Confidential'.
Actuary K is acting properly because harsh language ensures the Board pays attention to actuarial risks.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Para 2.3, members must treat colleagues, clients, and the public with dignity, courtesy, and professional respect. Professional critique must be evidence-based and objective, avoiding abusive personal disparagement.
explanationIncorrect: Confidentiality markers do not exempt an actuary from the ethical duty of professional courtesy.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 6.4 (Professional Indemnity Insurance)
question: Under PCS v4.0 Para 6.4, what is the mandatory requirement for actuaries who offer actuarial consulting services to the public in an independent capacity?
options: They only need insurance if their consulting fees exceed Rs. 1 Crore per client.

They should maintain adequate and appropriate Professional Indemnity Insurance (PII) cover, or ensure they are covered by an employer's policy, to protect clients against financial loss arising from professional negligence.
PII is strictly forbidden under Indian insurance law as an illegal bet on professional failure.
They must maintain a minimum personal cash balance of Rs. 10 Crores in a nationalized bank.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Para 6.4, practitioners must ensure appropriate Professional Indemnity Insurance (PII) is in place, commensurate with the scale and risks of the assignments undertaken, to safeguard public and client interests.
explanationIncorrect: PII is a fundamental risk management safeguard in public practice, ensuring financial recourse in cases of inadvertent error.

source: PCS v4.0, Para 7.2 (Successor Requesting Predecessor's Workpapers)
question: Actuary S succeeds Actuary P as the Appointed Actuary of a life insurer. Actuary S writes to Actuary P demanding all of Actuary P's internal working models and confidential client memos. How must Actuary P handle this request under PCS v4.0?
options: Actuary P must refuse to speak with Actuary S and block all email correspondence.

Actuary P must cooperate professionally in the transition, but proprietary working papers belong to the firm/client; Actuary P should provide necessary handover explanations and cannot disclose client confidential records without client consent.
Actuary P should demand a fee of Rs. 50 Lakhs from Actuary S before answering any technical questions.
Actuary P must immediately mail all original hard-drive backups to Actuary S without asking the client.
explanationCorrect: Under PCS v4.0 Para 7.2 and 7.4, the incumbent must cooperate and provide relevant professional information regarding the handover, while respecting client confidentiality and proprietary working paper rights.
explanationIncorrect: Handover cooperation requires professional assistance without unlawfully disclosing proprietary or unconsented client records.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 1(2) & Enactment
question: Which of the following statements regarding the legislative enactment and territorial commencement of the Actuaries Act, 2006 is legally accurate?
options: It is Act No. 35 of 2006 passed by Parliament, received Presidential assent on 27 August 2006, was officially notified to commence on 10 November 2006, and extends to the whole of India.
It is a state enactment passed by the Maharashtra Legislative Assembly that took effect on 1 January 2000 and applies only to financial institutions in Mumbai.
It is a delegated circular issued directly by IRDAI without parliamentary legislation.
It was enacted in 1944 under British colonial rule and applies exclusively to life insurance actuaries.
explanationCorrect: The Actuaries Act, 2006 is Act No. 35 of 2006 enacted by the Parliament of India. It received Presidential assent on 27 August 2006, commenced on 10 November 2006, and extends to the whole of India.
explanationIncorrect: The Act is primary Central parliamentary legislation, not a state law, historical colonial code, or regulatory circular.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 2(1)(a) (Definition of Actuary)
question: Under Section 2(1)(a) of the Actuaries Act 2006, what is the precise statutory definition of an 'Actuary'?
options: Any graduate with a master's degree in statistics or applied mathematics working in an insurance company.

A person skilled in determining the present effects of future contingent events or in finance modelling and risk analysis in different areas of financial, or other business, or socio-economic problems and for insurance and pension, and who is a Fellow member of the Institute.
Any individual who has cleared at least ten professional examination papers of the Institute of Actuaries of India.
A corporate executive appointed by the Board of Directors to manage underwriting margins.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 2(1)(a), an 'actuary' is statutorily defined as a person skilled in contingent financial modeling and risk analysis across finance, insurance, and pensions, AND who is a Fellow member (FIAI) of the Institute.
explanationIncorrect: Passing exam papers (Option B) or academic degrees (Option C) does not confer the statutory status of an Actuary without Fellowship admission.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 2(1)(b) (Definition of Appointed Actuary)
question: How does Section 2(1)(b) of the Actuaries Act 2006 define an 'Appointed Actuary'?
options: An actuary nominated by the Central Government to serve on the Appellate Authority.
A senior partner appointed by an audit firm to perform statutory financial accounting audits.
An actuary appointed by an insurer in accordance with the regulations made by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority (IRDAI).
An actuary elected by the Council of the Institute to supervise student examinations.
explanationCorrect: Section 2(1)(b) defines 'Appointed Actuary' specifically as an actuary appointed by an insurer in accordance with regulations made by the Authority (IRDAI).
explanationIncorrect: The Appointed Actuary is an insurer-specific statutory appointment governed by IRDAI Appointed Actuary Regulations.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 2(2) (Being in Practice)
question: Under Section 2(2) of the Actuaries Act 2006, when is a member deemed to be 'in practice'?
options: Only when the member has registered as an advocate before the High Court.
Only when the member is a full-time corporate employee of an insurance company receiving a monthly salary.

When, individually or in partnership with other actuaries, for remuneration, the member engages in actuarial science, offers to perform actuarial services, or renders professional service in actuarial matters.
Whenever a member reads actuarial textbooks or attends academic seminars.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 2(2), a member is deemed to be in practice if, in consideration of remuneration, they engage in actuarial science, offer actuarial services to the public, or render professional actuarial advice individually or in partnership.
explanationIncorrect: Full-time salaried employment (Option B) is distinct from public practice under Section 2(2).

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 3 & 4 (Incorporation & Dissolution of ASI)
question: What was the legal effect of Sections 3 and 4 of the Actuaries Act 2006 on the appointed day (10 November 2006)?
options: The Ministry of Finance took direct operational ownership of all member insurance liabilities.

The erstwhile Actuarial Society of India (ASI) was dissolved, and its assets, rights, liabilities, and contracts were statutorily transferred to and vested in the incorporated Institute of Actuaries of India (IAI).
The Actuarial Society of India continued to operate as an independent competing regulatory body.
The IAI was established as an unlisted private commercial company under the Companies Act 1956.
explanationCorrect: Under Sections 3 and 4, the statutory body corporate (IAI) was created with perpetual succession and common seal, while the pre-existing Actuarial Society of India (ASI) was dissolved, vesting all properties and liabilities into IAI.
explanationIncorrect: IAI is a statutory body created by an Act of Parliament, not a private company, and ASI ceased to exist upon statutory commencement.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 9(1) (Mandatory Certificate of Practice)
question: Under Section 9(1) of the Actuaries Act 2006, what is the mandatory statutory prerequisite for any member of the Institute to practice actuarial science in India?
options: The member must hold a valid, current Certificate of Practice (COP) granted by the Council.
The member must obtain a municipal commercial trade permit from the local civic corporation.
The member must register as an investment advisor with SEBI.
The member only needs to have passed the Fellowship examination and be current on annual subscription dues.
explanationCorrect: Section 9(1) states: 'No member of the Institute shall be entitled to practice unless he has obtained from the Council a certificate of practice.'
explanationIncorrect: Practicing without a valid COP issued by Council is an illegal act that attracts criminal prosecution under Section 38.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 11 (Removal from Register of Members)
question: Under Section 11 of the Actuaries Act 2006, which of the following is NOT a mandatory ground for the Council to remove a member's name from the Register of Members?
options: The member expresses a dissenting professional opinion regarding a draft Guidance Note during an AGM debate.
The member is declared to be of unsound mind by a court of competent jurisdiction.
The member has been convicted by a competent court of an offence involving moral turpitude.
The member is an undischarged insolvent.
explanationCorrect: Section 11 mandates removal for death, voluntary resignation, non-payment of dues, unsound mind, undischarged insolvency, conviction for moral turpitude/imprisonment, or disciplinary expulsion. Expressing dissenting professional opinions is legitimate debate and cannot be a ground for removal.
explanationIncorrect: Options B, C, and D are express statutory grounds for removal under Section 11(1).

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 12 (Council Composition)
question: Under Section 12 of the Actuaries Act 2006, what is the maximum statutory size of the Council and its mandated composition?
options: 10 members, consisting exclusively of Appointed Actuaries from state-owned insurers.
5 members, elected annually by student examinees.
Not more than 16 members: at least 9 elected by Fellows and Associates, up to 4 nominated by the Central Government, and up to 3 nominated/ex-officio members.
Exactly 25 members, all appointed directly by the Minister of Finance.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 12, the Council is capped at a maximum of 16 members, with a democratic majority of at least 9 members elected by members, supplemented by up to 4 Central Government nominees and up to 3 Council nominees.
explanationIncorrect: Options B, C, and D misrepresent the statutory democratic and regulatory balance of the Council.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 14 (Council Term of Office)
question: What is the statutory duration of the term of office for elected and nominated members of the Council under Section 14 of the Actuaries Act 2006?
options: Five years, matching the term of the Lok Sabha.
Three years (3 years) from the date of constitution of the Council.
A permanent lifetime appointment unless removed by impeachment.
One year, requiring annual nation-wide re-elections.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 14, Council members hold office for a term of 3 years from the date on which the Council is constituted.
explanationIncorrect: Office bearers (President, VP, Hon Secretary) serve 1-year terms under Sec 17, but the Council body as a whole serves a 3-year term under Sec 14.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 17 (Election of Office Bearers)
question: Under Section 17 of the Actuaries Act 2006, how are the President, Vice-President, and Honorary Secretary of the Institute chosen?
options: They are appointed directly by the Prime Minister's Office for a 5-year tenure.
They are nominated exclusively by the Central Government nominees on the Council.
They are elected by the Council from among its elected members for a term of one year.
They are selected by a random lottery of all practicing Fellows.
explanationCorrect: Section 17 provides that the Council shall, at its first meeting, elect from among its elected members a President, a Vice-President, and an Honorary Secretary for a term of one year.
explanationIncorrect: Central Government nominees cannot be elected as President or Vice-President; these office bearers must come from the democratically elected member pool.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 43 (Constitution of Quality Review Board)
question: Under Section 43 of the Actuaries Act 2006, who has the statutory authority to establish the Quality Review Board (QRB), and what is its composition?
options: The Supreme Court of India appoints the QRB as a judicial bench of retired judges.
The IRDAI Chairperson constitutes the QRB from among insurance brokers.
The President of the IAI establishes the QRB, consisting of 10 Fellows chosen at their sole discretion.
The Central Government constitutes the QRB, consisting of a Chairperson and 4 other members (2 nominated by Central Government, 2 nominated by Council).
explanationCorrect: Section 43(1) & (2) mandates that the Central Government shall constitute a Quality Review Board consisting of a Chairperson (an eminent person) and 4 other members (2 appointed by Central Govt, 2 appointed by Council).
explanationIncorrect: A common exam trap is assuming the IAI President or Council appoints the QRB. The QRB is an independent statutory body created directly by the Central Government.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 44 (Functions of the Quality Review Board)
question: Which of the following is a primary statutory function of the Quality Review Board under Section 44 of the Actuaries Act 2006?
options: To set examination papers and establish passing percentages for student members.
To negotiate commercial fee schedules between actuarial consulting firms and corporate clients.
To levy criminal imprisonment penalties on actuaries convicted of fraud.
To review the quality of services provided by members of the Institute (including actuarial audit services), fix standards, and guide members on improving quality.
explanationCorrect: Section 44 assigns three core functions to the QRB: (a) fix standards for services provided by members, (b) review service quality, including actuarial audit services, and (c) guide members on improving quality and statutory compliance.
explanationIncorrect: Examinations are handled by the Examination Committee, criminal punishment is judicial, and fee negotiation is a commercial matter outside QRB scope.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 38 (Penalty for Practicing Without COP)
question: An individual whose application for a Certificate of Practice was rejected continues to sign actuarial valuation reports claiming to be a practicing actuary. Upon first conviction under Section 38, what statutory penalty may the court impose?
options: A reprimand by the local police station with zero judicial record.
A monetary fine of Rs. 50,00,000 and seizure of all personal assets.
Mandatory capital punishment.
A fine which may extend to one thousand rupees (Rs. 1,000).
explanationCorrect: Section 38 provides that any person falsely claiming to be an actuary or practicing without a COP shall be punishable on first conviction with a fine up to Rs. 1,000.
explanationIncorrect: First conviction carries a statutory fine cap of Rs. 1,000; the harsher penalty of imprisonment up to 6 months and/or fine up to Rs. 5,000 applies only on subsequent conviction.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 38 (Subsequent Conviction Penalty)
question: Under Section 38 of the Actuaries Act 2006, what is the maximum criminal penalty for a person convicted of practicing without a COP on a second or subsequent conviction?
options: Imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with a fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.
Life imprisonment without possibility of parole.
A permanent ban on visiting the city of Mumbai.
Community service for 48 hours without any monetary fine.
explanationCorrect: Section 38 explicitly provides that on any subsequent conviction, the offender shall be punishable with imprisonment up to 6 months, or fine up to Rs. 5,000, or both.
explanationIncorrect: Subsequent conviction introduces potential custodial jail time (up to 6 months), escalating beyond the simple fine of the first conviction.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 39 (Penalty for Misuse of Institute Name)
question: Under Section 39 of the Actuaries Act 2006, what penalty may be imposed on an unaccredited private commercial coaching institute that awards a 'Diploma in Actuarial Science' falsely implying affiliation with or authorization from the IAI?
options: The coaching institute is automatically acquired by the Central Government.
Zero penalty, because commercial educational institutes are exempt from professional statutes.
A fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees (Rs. 10,000).
A mandatory fine of Rs. 1,00,000 per enrolled student.
explanationCorrect: Section 39 prohibits unauthorized use of the Institute's name, common seal, or awarding degrees/diplomas implying IAI accreditation, punishable with a fine up to Rs. 10,000.
explanationIncorrect: Commercial educational ventures cannot usurp the statutory monopoly of IAI in granting actuarial titles and diplomas.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 41 (Cognizance of Offences)
question: Under Section 41 of the Actuaries Act 2006, which court may try offences under the Act, and on whose complaint may cognizance be taken?
options: Any village Panchayat court, on a verbal complaint by any citizen.
Exclusively the Supreme Court of India on a Public Interest Litigation (PIL).
A commercial consumer dispute forum, on a complaint by an insurance policyholder.
No court inferior to that of a Metropolitan Magistrate or a Judicial Magistrate of the first class, and only on a complaint made by or under the order of the Council or the Central Government.
explanationCorrect: Section 41 mandates that only a Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of the First Class can try statutory offences, and courts can only take cognizance upon a formal complaint from the Council or Central Government.
explanationIncorrect: Private individuals cannot initiate direct criminal prosecution under the Act without Council or Central Government authorization.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 56 (Regulations Making Power)
question: Under Section 56 of the Actuaries Act 2006, can the Council make regulations altering examination structures, fees, or membership procedures independently?
options: No; regulations can only be drafted and enacted directly by the Reserve Bank of India.
Yes; the Council is an autonomous sovereign body and requires no government approval for regulations.
No; the Council makes regulations by notification in the Official Gazette, but strictly with the prior approval of the Central Government.
Yes, provided 100% of Fellow members vote in favor in a national referendum.
explanationCorrect: Section 56(1) states: 'The Council may, by notification in the Official Gazette, make regulations with the prior approval of the Central Government to carry out the provisions of this Act.'
explanationIncorrect: A critical statutory check and balance: Council cannot promulgate binding subordinate regulations without prior Central Government approval.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 19(2)(i) (Power to Prescribe Standards)
question: Which specific provision of the Actuaries Act 2006 confers legal authority upon the Council to issue mandatory Actuarial Practice Standards (APSs) and the Professional Conduct Standards (PCS)?
options: Section 43, establishing the Quality Review Board.
Section 19(2)(i), empowering Council to prescribe professional standards and codes of conduct.
Section 2(1)(a), defining the skills of an actuary.
Section 38, governing criminal penalties for designation misuse.
explanationCorrect: Section 19(2)(i) is the specific statutory anchor authorizing Council to establish, maintain, and enforce professional and technical standards, including PCS v4.0 and all Actuarial Practice Standards.
explanationIncorrect: Breach of standards issued under Section 19(2)(i) constitutes professional misconduct under the Schedules of the Act.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 7 (Register of Members Voting Rights)
question: Under the Actuaries Act 2006, which classes of members are legally entitled to vote in Council elections under Section 12?
options: Exclusively Fellows holding a Certificate of Practice (COP).
Only corporate insurance companies that contribute annual sponsorship fees.
Fellows and Associates whose names are entered on the Register of Members.
All registered members, including student members and honorary affiliates.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 12(1)(a) and Section 6, the electorate for Council comprises Fellows and Associates. Students, honorary, and affiliate members do not possess statutory voting rights in Council elections.
explanationIncorrect: A common trap is assuming only COP holders vote. Both non-COP Fellows and Associates have statutory voting rights.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 11(2) (Restoration to Register of Members)
question: A member whose name was removed from the Register for non-payment of annual membership fees pays all arrears and the prescribed penalty. How is the member restored under Section 11(2)?
options: The Council may, on an application made by the member and on payment of the prescribed arrears and fees, restore the member's name to the Register.
The member's name can never be restored under any circumstances once removed.
The member must re-sit and clear all actuarial examination papers from the beginning.
Restoration requires a special statutory order issued directly by the Parliament of India.
explanationCorrect: Section 11(2) empowers Council to restore a member's name to the Register upon formal application, clearance of unpaid subscription arrears, and payment of the prescribed restoration fee.
explanationIncorrect: Re-sitting exams or parliamentary bills are absurd; administrative restoration is standard upon debt clearance.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 8 (Qualifications for Entry in Register)
question: Under Section 8 of the Actuaries Act 2006, what is required for an individual to have their name entered in the Register of Members as a Fellow?
options: The individual must be appointed as a director of an Indian insurance company.

The individual must have passed the prescribed examinations conducted by the Institute (or recognized equivalent examinations) and satisfied the requisite criteria of practical actuarial work experience.
The individual must pay an admission fee of Rs. 10 Lakhs without sitting for any examinations.
The individual only needs to be a graduate of an Indian university with mathematics as an elective subject.
explanationCorrect: Section 8 specifies the professional qualification criteria: passing prescribed professional examinations and satisfying the practical work experience requirement stipulated by Council regulations.
explanationIncorrect: Fellowship is an earned credential requiring exam success and practical experience, not an honorary title or commercial purchase.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 13 (Resignation of Council Members)
question: Under Section 13 of the Actuaries Act 2006, to whom must an elected Council member submit their written resignation if they wish to resign from Council, and when does it take effect?
options: Council members are statutorily prohibited from ever resigning during their 3-year term.
To the President of the Council, and it takes effect on the date on which it is accepted by the Council.
To the Chief Election Commissioner of India, taking effect immediately upon posting.
To the local police commissioner within 24 hours.
explanationCorrect: Section 13 provides that a member of the Council may resign their seat by giving notice in writing to the President, taking effect when accepted by the Council.
explanationIncorrect: Resignation is an orderly statutory procedure addressed to the President of the Council.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 14 (Casual Vacancies in Council)
question: When an elected Council member dies or resigns midway through their 3-year term, creating a casual vacancy, how is the seat filled under Section 14 of the Act?
options: A nation-wide general election must be conducted within 48 hours.
The seat remains permanently vacant until the next 3-year election cycle.
The President's eldest family member automatically inherits the Council seat.
The Council fills the casual vacancy by nomination from amongst the members of the Institute who are eligible for election, and the appointed member holds office for the remainder of the term.
explanationCorrect: Section 14(3) empowers Council to fill casual vacancies among elected seats by nominating an eligible member from the Register, who serves out the unexpired portion of the 3-year term.
explanationIncorrect: Mid-term casual vacancies do not trigger costly nation-wide general elections.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 15 (Meetings of Council & Quorum)
question: Under Section 15 of the Actuaries Act 2006 and Council Regulations, what is the statutory frequency of Council meetings and the quorum required?
options: The Council meets once every five years with a quorum of two members.
The Council meets daily, with 100% attendance mandatory.
The Council must meet at least once in every three months, and the quorum for a meeting is one-third of the total number of members of the Council.
Meetings are only convened if summoned by the President of India.
explanationCorrect: Section 15 and regulations mandate regular quarterly governance meetings (at least once every 3 months), requiring a one-third quorum of Council members to transact business lawfully.
explanationIncorrect: Quarterly meetings ensure ongoing executive oversight over examination, standard-setting, and disciplinary functions.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 24 (Finances & Statutory Audit)
question: Under Section 24 of the Actuaries Act 2006, how are the annual financial accounts of the Institute audited?
options: The accounts are audited by an insurance loss assessor appointed by IRDAI.
The accounts are exempt from all financial audit requirements under sovereign prerogative.
The accounts are audited internally by actuarial students sitting for core exams.
The accounts must be audited annually by a Chartered Accountant in practice holding a valid COP from the ICAI, appointed annually by the Council.
explanationCorrect: Section 24(2) mandates that the accounts of the Institute shall be audited annually by a Chartered Accountant in practice, ensuring independent external verification of Institute funds.
explanationIncorrect: Statutory accounting audits require independent Chartered Accountants under ICAI standards.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 35 (Bar of Jurisdiction of Civil Courts)
question: Under Section 35 of the Actuaries Act 2006, can a member facing disciplinary inquiry file a civil lawsuit in a local municipal court seeking an injunction to stop the Disciplinary Committee from meeting?
options: Yes; any civil judge can issue a stay order halting actuarial disciplinary proceedings at will.
Yes, provided the member pays a court fee of Rs. 100.

No; Section 35 explicitly bars the jurisdiction of Civil Courts to entertain any suit or proceeding in respect of any matter which the Council, Board of Discipline, or Disciplinary Committee is empowered to determine.
Civil courts automatically supersede all statutory professional tribunals in India.
explanationCorrect: Section 35 creates a statutory bar on civil court intervention: civil courts have no jurisdiction over matters entrusted by Parliament to the Disciplinary Directorate, Board of Discipline, or Disciplinary Committee.
explanationIncorrect: Disciplinary decisions can only be challenged through the statutory appellate mechanism (Section 36) and constitutional writ jurisdiction.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 42 (Protection of Action Taken in Good Faith)
question: If a member who was reprimanded by the Board of Discipline attempts to sue the individual members of the Board of Discipline for personal monetary damages in tort, how does Section 42 protect the Board members?
options: Statutory immunity only applies if the member was acquitted.
Board members must personally pay damages from their personal bank accounts.
Protection applies only if the Board members are also advocates registered with the Bar Council.

Section 42 provides complete statutory immunity: no suit, prosecution, or legal proceeding shall lie against the Council, Board of Discipline, Disciplinary Committee, or officers for anything done in good faith under the Act.
explanationCorrect: Section 42 contains the classic statutory protection clause: officers, Council members, and disciplinary tribunal members enjoy complete legal immunity for actions taken in good faith in discharge of their statutory duties.
explanationIncorrect: Statutory immunity ensures disciplinary authorities can adjudicate without fear of personal retaliatory lawsuits.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 55 (Central Government Directions)
question: Under Section 55 of the Actuaries Act 2006, what is the legal effect of a policy directive issued by the Central Government to the Council of the Institute?
options: The Council may discard government policy directions if 51% of members vote against them.
The Council can only follow directions if approved by the International Actuarial Association.
Central Government directions are merely non-binding informal recommendations with zero legal force.

The Council must, in the exercise of its functions, be guided by such directions on questions of policy as may be given to it in writing by the Central Government, and the decision of the Central Government on whether a question is one of policy is final.
explanationCorrect: Section 55 affirms sovereign parliamentary supremacy: the Central Government may issue binding policy directives in writing, and its determination of whether a matter constitutes policy is final.
explanationIncorrect: Professional self-regulation operates within the statutory boundaries established by the Central Government.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 19(2)(d) (Management of Institute Funds)
question: Under Section 19(2)(d) of the Actuaries Act 2006, how must the Council manage and invest the surplus funds of the Institute?
options: In accordance with investment guidelines and prudent trustee standards in securities of the Central Government or approved scheduled commercial banks.
By lending money to corporate insurance companies at high interest rates.
By investing in speculative cryptocurrency derivatives on overseas exchanges.
Council members may distribute surplus funds as personal annual cash dividends among themselves.
explanationCorrect: Section 19(2)(d) mandates prudent management and safe investment of Institute funds in approved securities and government-backed avenues, preserving the Institute's financial security.
explanationIncorrect: Institute funds are public statutory property dedicated to advancing the actuarial profession, not for speculative trading or member dividends.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 37 (Maintenance of Register of Members)
question: Who is statutorily responsible for maintaining the Register of Members of the Institute under Section 6 and Chapter II of the Act?
options: The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority (IRDAI) head office in Hyderabad.
The Ministry of Corporate Affairs in New Delhi.
A private third-party recruitment staffing agency.
The Council of the Institute, acting through its Secretariat and designated officers.
explanationCorrect: Chapter II of the Act establishes that the Register of Members is maintained directly by the Council of the Institute of Actuaries of India.
explanationIncorrect: Custodianship of the roll of professionals is a defining attribute of the statutory self-regulatory body.

source: IAI Governance, Section 21 Standing Committees
question: Under Section 21 of the Actuaries Act 2006, how many active executive Standing Committees are currently constituted by the Council to manage the operational and policy functions of the Institute?
options: Twelve (12) standing committees corresponding to each of the Practice Advisory Groups.
Six (6) active Standing Committees: Professionalism, Audit, Finance/HR/IT/Admin, Education and Examination, Research and Innovation, and Student Growth and Success.
Eight (8) regional standing committees managing state-level chapters across India.
Only three committees: an Executive Committee, an Examination Committee, and a Disciplinary Committee.
explanationCorrect: The Council operates through 6 active Section 21 Standing Committees: (1) Professionalism, (2) Audit, (3) Finance, HR, IT & Admin, (4) Education & Examination, (5) Research & Innovation, and (6) Student Growth & Success.
explanationIncorrect: The 6 Section 21 Standing Committees form the administrative executive engine of the Institute.

source: IAI Governance, Section 21 Professionalism Committee
question: Which Section 21 Standing Committee acts as the custodian of professional conduct, reviews interpretations of PCS v4.0, and monitors compliance with ethical guidance notes across the Institute?
options: The Practice Advisory Group on Banking and Investments.
The Student Growth and Success Committee.
The Professionalism Committee.
The Audit Committee.
explanationCorrect: The Professionalism Committee is the specific Section 21 executive standing committee charged with overseeing professional standards, ethical interpretations of PCS, and guidance notes.
explanationIncorrect: The Audit Committee oversees internal financial controls, Student Growth focuses on candidate mentoring, and PAGs are advisory think-tanks.

source: IAI Governance, Section 21 Audit Committee
question: What is the statutory and operational responsibility of the Audit Committee constituted by Council under Section 21?
options: Auditing policyholder reserves of commercial insurance companies on behalf of the IRDAI.
Overseeing the financial reporting integrity of the Institute, reviewing internal financial controls, supervising statutory external audits, and assessing enterprise risk management.
Conducting forensic investigations into allegations of student examination cheating.
Fixing statutory premium tariffs for general insurance third-party motor liability.
explanationCorrect: The Audit Committee is an internal oversight committee ensuring fiscal integrity, reviewing internal financial controls, and supervising the annual statutory audit of the Institute itself.
explanationIncorrect: Commercial insurance reserves are audited by statutory financial auditors and reviewed by the QRB, not the IAI internal Audit Committee.

source: IAI Governance, Practice Advisory Groups (PAGs) Count & Function
question: How many Practice Advisory Groups (PAGs) are established under the IAI governance framework to provide domain-specific technical leadership and advice?
options: Six (6) advisory groups matching the number of Section 21 Standing Committees.
Twenty-four (24) advisory groups covering each distinct actuarial examination subject.
Exactly twelve (12) Practice Advisory Groups spanning specialized technical areas such as Life, General Insurance, Health, Pensions, Banking, and Risk Management.
Four (4) advisory groups corresponding to the four primary insurance licensing classes.
explanationCorrect: There are currently 12 Practice Advisory Groups (PAGs) serving as domain-specific technical think-tanks, drafting guidance notes, and advising Council on regulatory policy.
explanationIncorrect: 12 PAGs provide specialized coverage across Life, GI, Health, Pensions, ERM, Banking, Agriculture, and broader domains.

source: IAI Governance, PAG on Life Insurance Remit
question: Which Practice Advisory Group is primarily responsible for drafting Guidance Notes and Actuarial Practice Standards on statutory reserving (APS 2), solvency margin monitoring, and participating with-profits management?
options: The Practice Advisory Group on Life Insurance.
The Practice Advisory Group on Sustainable Development and Microinsurance.
The Practice Advisory Group on Risk Management.
The Practice Advisory Group on Banking, Finance & Investments.
explanationCorrect: The Life Insurance PAG focuses on technical standards, valuation regulations, product pricing guidelines, and asset-liability matching for life insurers.
explanationIncorrect: Other PAGs focus on non-life reserving, banking models, or general enterprise risk management.

source: IAI Governance, PAG on General Insurance Remit
question: Which Practice Advisory Group leads technical research on IBNR/IBNER reserving methodologies, claims development triangles, and pricing models for non-life lines?
options: The Practice Advisory Group on Communication.
The Practice Advisory Group on General Insurance.
The Practice Advisory Group on Agriculture and Rural Risk.
The Practice Advisory Group on Health Care Insurance.
explanationCorrect: The General Insurance PAG provides technical leadership on non-life reserving, stochastic claims triangulation, catastrophic risk modeling, and motor third-party pools.
explanationIncorrect: The GI PAG advises both Council and IRDAI on property and casualty technical regulations.

source: IAI Governance, Specialized Working Groups Mandate
question: How do Specialized Working Groups (WGs)—such as the Working Group on IFRS 17 (Ind AS 117) and the Working Group on AI & Data Science—differ from permanent Standing Committees?
options: Working Groups are composed entirely of external government officials from the Ministry of Finance.
Working Groups are task-oriented, cross-functional expert bodies formed by Council to address urgent emerging regulatory, accounting, or technological shifts.
Working Groups have statutory powers under the Actuaries Act to issue legally binding penal sanctions against members.
Working Groups operate completely independently of Council and report directly to Parliament.
explanationCorrect: Working Groups are ad-hoc or specialized bodies formed to resolve complex, emerging industry transitions (e.g. Ind AS 117 implementation, algorithmic AI ethics, climate risk).
explanationIncorrect: They advise Council and produce technical guidance, but do not possess independent statutory regulatory power.

source: IAI Governance, Working Group on IFRS 17 (Ind AS 117)
question: What is the primary technical objective of the IAI Working Group on IFRS 17 (Ind AS 117)?
options: Formulating actuarial guidance on transition methods, contract boundaries, discounting yield curves, and liability measurement models in convergence with Indian accounting standards.
Administering corporate tax compliance for general insurance underwriting pools.
Auditing the commercial software licensing agreements of domestic insurance companies.
Setting statutory interest rates for national small savings schemes.
explanationCorrect: The IFRS 17 Working Group focuses on actuarial technicalities under Ind AS 117: discount curve determination (CCIL curve), risk adjustment percentiles, PAA eligibility, and CSM emergence.
explanationIncorrect: It liaises directly with ICAI, IRDAI, and industry bodies on financial reporting harmonization.

source: IAI Governance, Quality Review Board (QRB) Statutory Pedigree
question: Under Section 43 of the Actuaries Act 2006, how is the Quality Review Board (QRB) constituted, and what is its statutory tenure?
options: Sub-committee of the Disciplinary Committee comprising three members holding office for one year.
Advisory council appointed by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority holding office at pleasure.
Internal committee appointed by the Council President, comprising five Fellows holding office for five years.
Constitutional body appointed by the Central Government, comprising a Chairperson and four (4) other members, holding office for a term of three (3) years.
explanationCorrect: Section 43 vests the appointment of the QRB directly in the Central Government: a Chairperson plus 4 members (2 nominated by Central Govt, 2 by Council), with a 3-year term.
explanationIncorrect: The QRB is an independent external statutory supervisor, not an internal Council committee.

source: IAI Governance, Statutory Functions of the QRB
question: Under Section 44 of the Actuaries Act 2006, which of the following is NOT one of the three primary statutory functions of the Quality Review Board?
options: To guide members of the Institute on improving the quality of services and adhering to statutory regulations.
To impose monetary fines and issue suspension orders against individual actuaries found guilty of professional negligence.
To fix standards for services provided by the members of the Institute.
To review the quality of services provided by the members of the Institute, including actuarial audit services.
explanationCorrect: Section 44 lists three functions: (a) fixing service standards, (b) reviewing service quality, and (c) guiding members. The QRB CANNOT impose disciplinary penalties; it reports findings to Council.
explanationIncorrect: Disciplinary sanctions are the exclusive statutory domain of the Board of Discipline and Disciplinary Committee under Chapter IV.

source: IAI Governance, Council Guidelines for Conducting Annual General Meetings (AGM)
question: Under Council guidelines approved on 02 March 2013, what is the mandatory notice period required for convening an Annual General Meeting (AGM) of the Institute?
options: At least forty-five (45) days' notice published in national business newspapers.
At least seven (7) calendar days' notice delivered by registered post.
At least ninety (90) days' notice matching the disciplinary appeal limitation window.
At least twenty-one (21) clear days' written notice specifying the date, time, venue, and agenda items.
explanationCorrect: Under the Council Guidelines for AGMs, at least 21 clear days' notice must be provided to all eligible members before the meeting can lawfully proceed.
explanationIncorrect: 21 clear days provides sufficient time for members to review annual accounts and submit formal resolutions or proxy votes.

source: IAI Governance, Standard-Setting Due Process (Consultation Period)
question: Under the Council's Standard Setting Due Process (Versions 3, 4, 5), for what duration must an Exposure Draft of a proposed Actuarial Practice Standard (APS) be published on the IAI website for public consultation?
options: Public consultation is optional; standards may be enacted without public exposure if approved unanimously by Council.
For exactly seven (7) calendar days prior to final Council enactment.
For a minimum of one full calendar year (365 days).
For a consultation window of thirty (30) to sixty (60) days to solicit comments from members, industry stakeholders, and regulators.
explanationCorrect: The Due Process mandates a 30 to 60-day public exposure period for draft standards, ensuring rigorous transparency, stakeholder review, and technical debate.
explanationIncorrect: Robust due process ensures that newly enacted APSs reflect broad consensus and regulatory alignment.

source: IAI Governance, Annual Report & Audited Accounts Presentation
question: Under the Actuaries Act 2006 and Council Governance Guidelines, where must the annual report of Council activities and audited financial accounts be formally presented to members?
options: At the opening session of the Global Conference of Actuaries.
At the Annual General Meeting (AGM) of the Institute convened within prescribed statutory timelines.
Exclusively in a confidential circular sent to the Ministry of Corporate Affairs.
At a quarterly meeting of the Professionalism Committee.
explanationCorrect: Under standard governance rules, the annual report and audited balance sheet must be formally laid before members at the Annual General Meeting (AGM) following at least 21 clear days' notice.
explanationIncorrect: Democratic transparency requires annual accounts to be presented directly to the voting membership.

source: IAI Governance, Practice Advisory Group (PAG) Composition
question: Who typically chairs and comprises a Practice Advisory Group (PAG) within the IAI institutional framework?
options: A member of the Quality Review Board acting as permanent ex-officio chair.
A Chairperson who is a senior Fellow with recognized domain expertise, supported by appointed members with relevant technical practice experience.
A senior representative from the Ministry of Law and Justice.
Any Associate member who submits the earliest formal expression of interest.
explanationCorrect: PAGs are chaired by experienced Fellows appointed by Council, drawing upon qualified actuarial practitioners and domain specialists to drive technical excellence in that vertical.
explanationIncorrect: PAGs require senior practice leadership to maintain rigorous technical dialogues with IRDAI and global standard-setters.
