explanationIncorrect: Recusal ensures the tribunal remains impartial and free from real or perceived bias.

source: Student Code of Conduct (2026), Relationship with Actuaries Act 2006
question: What is the statutory basis empowering the Council of the Institute to formulate and enforce the Student Code of Conduct (2026)?
options: The Indian Contract Act 1872 governing private tuition contracts.
An executive notification issued directly by the University Grants Commission.
The overarching statutory powers of the Council under Section 19 and Section 56 of the Actuaries Act 2006 to regulate the education, training, and discipline of students.
A delegation of authority from the Central Board of Secondary Education.
explanationCorrect: The Student Code derives statutory legitimacy from Section 19 and Section 56 of the Actuaries Act 2006, empowering Council to regulate the education, examinations, and disciplinary control over candidates.
explanationIncorrect: The Actuaries Act 2006 provides the plenary statutory foundation for all student conduct regulations.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Section 3 & Compliance Year
question: Under Actuarial Practice Standard 9 (APS 9 v4.00: Continuing Professional Development), what is the official statutory CPD compliance year?
options: A three-year block matching the cyclical peer review audit schedule.
From 1st April of a calendar year to 31st March of the immediately following calendar year.
A rolling twelve-month window measured from the date of the member's admission to Fellowship.
From 1st January to 31st December (standard calendar year).
explanationCorrect: Under APS 9 Section 3, the CPD compliance year runs concurrently with the Indian financial year, from 1st April to 31st March annually.
explanationIncorrect: Annual CPD compliance is assessed on the 1 April – 31 March financial year basis, not on calendar years or rolling anniversaries.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Section 4.4.3 (Category 1 COP Holder Mandatory Hours)
question: Under APS 9 Section 4.4.3, what is the mandatory annual CPD requirement for a Category 1 actuary (Fellow holding a Certificate of Practice)?
options: A minimum of 40 verifiable hours with no specific allocation between technical and professional content.
Exactly 15 verifiable CPD hours per year, consisting entirely of general corporate governance seminars.
A minimum of 30 verifiable CPD hours per year: at least 20 technical and 10 professional conduct.
A minimum of 24 verifiable CPD hours per year: at least 15 technical in primary practice area, at least 6 professional conduct & ethics, and maximum 3 other verifiable hours.
explanationCorrect: Section 4.4.3 establishes the 24-hour mandatory triad for COP holders: minimum 15 hours technical in designated primary practice area, minimum 6 hours professional/ethical conduct, and maximum 3 hours other verifiable learning.
explanationIncorrect: A Category 1 COP holder must satisfy all three sub-allocations within their 24 verifiable hours.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Section 4.1.4 (Multiple Practice Areas Rule)
question: An actuary holds a Certificate of Practice (Category 1) and actively signs statutory valuations in both Life Insurance and Health Insurance. Under Section 4.1.4 of APS 9, what is the actuary's total mandatory annual CPD requirement?
options: 30 verifiable hours, adding a flat 6-hour general administration allowance.
48 verifiable hours, obtained by fully doubling the entire 24-hour annual requirement.
24 verifiable hours total, because the base 24 hours covers all practice areas combined.
32 verifiable CPD hours: 24 base hours (including min 15 Life technical + 6 professional) plus an additional 8 verifiable technical hours in Health Insurance.
explanationCorrect: Section 4.1.4 mandates that a COP holder practicing in more than one practice area must complete an additional 8 verifiable technical CPD hours for EACH supplementary practice area (24 + 8 = 32 hours).
explanationIncorrect: A classic numerical exam trap: you add 8 technical hours per additional area, rather than doubling the entire requirement or doing nothing.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Section 4.1.4 (Three Practice Areas Calculation)
question: A senior consulting actuary holds a COP and signs formal statutory reports across three distinct practice areas: General Insurance (primary), Life Insurance, and Pensions. What is their total annual verifiable CPD requirement?
options: 40 verifiable CPD hours (24 base hours + 8 Life technical + 8 Pensions technical).
36 verifiable hours, based on a flat 12 hours per practice area.
24 verifiable hours total, provided the professional conduct hours are doubled.
72 verifiable hours, calculated as 24 hours multiplied by 3 practice areas.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 4.1.4, with General Insurance as primary (24 base hours), each of the two additional areas (Life and Pensions) requires an additional 8 technical hours: 24 + 8 + 8 = 40 verifiable CPD hours.
explanationIncorrect: Multi-practice practitioners must maintain specialized technical currency in each vertical they sign.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Section 4.5 (Category 2 Active Fellows without COP)
question: Under Section 4.5 of APS 9, what is the mandatory annual CPD requirement for a Category 2 member (an active Fellow employed in a corporate, regulatory, or academic role who does NOT hold a Certificate of Practice)?
options: 10 verifiable hours consisting entirely of non-technical management seminars.
A minimum of 15 verifiable CPD hours per year: at least 9 technical, at least 3 professional conduct, and maximum 3 other verifiable hours.
Zero verifiable hours, because CPD is strictly voluntary for non-practicing Fellows.
24 verifiable hours per year, identical to Category 1 Certificate of Practice holders.
explanationCorrect: Section 4.5 sets the requirement for Category 2 active Fellows without a COP at 15 verifiable hours: min 9 technical, min 3 professional conduct, and max 3 other learning.
explanationIncorrect: Active Fellows without a COP have a reduced threshold (15 hours vs 24 hours) because they do not sign public statutory certificates.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Section 4.6 (Category 3 Inactive / Retired Fellows)
question: Under Section 4.6 of APS 9, how may a fully retired Fellow who has completely ceased actuarial professional work obtain exemption from annual CPD obligations?
options: By applying in writing to the Institute for Category 3 (Inactive Status) at least three (3) months prior to the end of the membership year.
Retired actuaries are legally prohibited from claiming exemption under any circumstances.
By filing a certified copy of their pension payment order with the local tax department.
Automatically upon reaching 60 years of age without submitting any written application.
explanationCorrect: Section 4.6 requires fully retired/inactive Fellows to apply formally in writing for Category 3 status at least 3 months before year-end to be granted CPD exemption.
explanationIncorrect: Exemption is not automatic upon reaching retirement age; formal application and approval are required.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Section 9.2 (Daily CPD Conversion Scale: 4 Hours Net)
question: An actuary attends a technical reinsurance seminar from 10:00 AM to 3:30 PM (5.5 hours total elapsed time), which includes a 1.5-hour lunch and networking break. Under Section 9.2 of APS 9, how many verifiable CPD hours are awarded?
options: 4 CPD hours (Actual net duration = 4.0 hours, which falls in the bracket '3.5 hours to less than 4.5 hours' = 4 CPD hours).
5.5 CPD hours, because all elapsed time spent at the professional venue is credited.
3 CPD hours, applying a statutory deduction for external sponsorship.
6 CPD hours, representing the maximum single-day seminar credit.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 9.2, meal breaks and receptions are strictly excluded. Net duration = 5.5h - 1.5h = 4.0 hours. The conversion table specifies: 3.5h to < 4.5h awards exactly 4 CPD hours.
explanationIncorrect: Elapsed gross time cannot be claimed; only net formal presentation/instruction time qualifies.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Section 9.2 (Maximum Daily CPD Credit Cap)
question: An actuary attends an intensive 9-hour technical actuarial conference with 7.5 hours of net formal lecture time in a single calendar day. Under Section 9.2 of APS 9, what is the maximum CPD credit that can be awarded for that single day?
options: 7.5 CPD hours, matching the exact net minutes of technical lecture time.
8 CPD hours, matching the standard working day calculation.
Six (6) CPD hours, which represents the absolute statutory daily ceiling under the scale (awarded for 5.5 hours or more).
Zero CPD hours, because single-day conferences exceeding 7 hours are invalid.
explanationCorrect: Section 9.2 establishes an absolute daily cap of 6 CPD hours for any formal event lasting 5.5 hours or more. No single day can generate more than 6 CPD hours.
explanationIncorrect: The 6-hour daily cap prevents cramming annual requirements into an unrealistic single session.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Section 9.2 (Sub-30 Minute Session Exclusion)
question: An actuary attends a 25-minute online vendor presentation introducing a new capital modeling tool. Under the discrete conversion table in Section 9.2 of APS 9, how many CPD hours are credited?
options: 0.5 CPD hour, rounded up to the nearest half hour.
1.0 CPD hour, under the standard minimum session rule.
0.25 CPD hour, calculated pro rata based on elapsed minutes.
Zero (0) CPD hours; the conversion table awards 0 credit for sessions lasting less than 0.5 hour (< 30 minutes).
explanationCorrect: Under Section 9.2, sessions of less than 30 minutes (< 0.5 hour) receive 0 CPD hours. Minimum qualifying threshold for 1 CPD hour is 30 to 89 minutes (0.5h to < 1.5h).
explanationIncorrect: Micro-sessions below 30 minutes do not award partial or fractional CPD hours.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Section 11.1 (Annual Self-Attestation Deadline)
question: Under Section 11.1 of APS 9, by what annual calendar deadline must an actuary submit their online CPD self-attestation and record of hours on the IAI member portal?
options: By 31st March (on the final day of the compliance year).
No later than 31st May (within two months of the end of the compliance year).
By 1st July, concurrent with the defaulters list publication.
By 30th April (within thirty days of the financial year-end).
explanationCorrect: Section 11.1 gives members a 2-month window following the close of the compliance year (31 March) to submit their online self-attestation, making the deadline strictly 31st May.
explanationIncorrect: 31 March is year-end; 31 May is the attestation deadline; 1 July is the public website defaulter listing.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Section 10.2 (Preservation of CPD Records)
question: Under Section 10.2 of APS 9, for what minimum period must members preserve all documentary evidence (attendance certificates, event agendas, registration receipts) supporting their CPD self-attestations?
options: Three (3) years from the date of the event.
One (1) year after submission of the online attestation.
Seven (7) years under ICAI SA 230 audit documentation standards.
A minimum period of at least five (5) years from the end of the relevant compliance year.
explanationCorrect: Section 10.2 requires members to preserve all physical and electronic CPD evidence for at least 5 years, for random audit inspection by the Council.
explanationIncorrect: CRITICAL EXAM TRAP: CPD records must be kept for 5 years (APS 9 Sec 10.2), whereas statutory audit working papers must be kept for 7 years (FT-IGN 31 / SA 230).

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Section 12.2 (Public Website Defaulter Listing Date)
question: Under Section 12.2 of APS 9, on what specific calendar date does the Institute publish the names of members who failed to comply with CPD requirements or submit self-attestations on the official IAI website?
options: 31st May (immediately upon expiry of the attestation window).
15th August (coinciding with the national holiday).
31st March of the compliance year.
1st July of the compliance reporting year.
explanationCorrect: Section 12.2 specifies that the list of non-compliant members and attestation defaulters is published on the official IAI website on 1st July.
explanationIncorrect: Public disclosure on 1st July provides market transparency to clients and insurers regarding an actuary's practice standing.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Section 12 (Sanctions for Category 1 CPD Non-Compliance)
question: What are the immediate professional consequences for a Category 1 actuary who defaults on their mandatory CPD requirements under APS 9 Section 12?
options: Immediate non-renewal of their Certificate of Practice (COP), suspension of statutory signing rights, and referral to the Director (Discipline) under the First Schedule.
A flat monetary fine of Rs. 10,000 with unconditional renewal of practicing rights.
Suspension of voting rights in Council elections without affecting client signing rights.
Mandatory re-examination in Subject SA2 (Life Insurance Specialist Applications).
explanationCorrect: Section 12 imposes severe sanctions on COP defaulters: their COP is not renewed, they cannot sign statutory valuations, and default is referred to the Director (Discipline) as professional misconduct.
explanationIncorrect: Maintaining CPD currency is an indispensable statutory condition for holding a valid COP.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Resumption of Practice after Inactive Status
question: A retired Fellow holding Category 3 (Inactive Status) wishes to resume active consulting practice and apply for a Certificate of Practice (COP). What is required under APS 9 Section 4.6?
options: The member can immediately resume practice provided they pay all back-dated membership dues.
The member must practice under the supervision of a junior Associate for twelve months.
The member must re-sit and pass the India Fellowship Seminar (IFS) examination.
The member must complete catch-up CPD requirements prescribed by Council in their practice area before a Certificate of Practice can be granted.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 4.6, an inactive member wishing to resume active practice must satisfy Council-prescribed catch-up CPD to demonstrate current technical and ethical competence before a COP is reissued.
explanationIncorrect: Catch-up learning ensures returning practitioners are abreast of contemporary regulations (such as Ind AS 117).

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Professional Conduct CPD Content Scope
question: Which of the following topics satisfies the mandatory requirement for 'Professional Conduct & Ethics' CPD (minimum 6 hours for Category 1 COP holders) under APS 9?
options: A technical masterclass on machine learning algorithms in general insurance pricing.
An internal team training session on Python data scraping and SQL database queries.
A structured seminar analyzing PCS v4.0 case studies, conflict of interest management, whistleblowing protocols, and the Actuaries Act disciplinary process.
A symposium on commercial real estate yield curves and sovereign debt trends.
explanationCorrect: Professional conduct CPD must cover professional ethics, PCS interpretations, conflicts of interest, disciplinary case law, statutory duties, or the India Fellowship Seminar (IFS).
explanationIncorrect: Technical mathematical modeling counts toward the technical quota, not the mandatory 6-hour professional conduct quota.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Carry-Forward of Surplus CPD Hours
question: An active Category 1 actuary completes 38 verifiable CPD hours during the 2024-25 compliance year, exceeding the mandatory 24-hour threshold by 14 hours. How are the surplus hours treated under APS 9?
options: Surplus CPD hours cannot be carried forward to any subsequent compliance year; every compliance year stands on its own.
Surplus technical hours may be converted into professional conduct hours in the following year.
All 14 surplus hours can be banked in a reserve account valid for up to three years.
Up to 10 surplus hours may be carried forward to the immediately following compliance year.
explanationCorrect: APS 9 strictly prohibits carrying forward surplus CPD hours to subsequent compliance years. CPD is an annual commitment designed to ensure continuous learning throughout each financial year.
explanationIncorrect: Each compliance year is an independent assessment period; excess hours lapse at year-end.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), International CPD Reciprocity
question: An Indian Fellow residing in London completes 30 hours of verifiable technical CPD accredited by the Institute and Faculty of Actuaries (IFoA). Can these hours be claimed towards IAI APS 9 compliance?
options: No; only CPD events physically organized within the territory of India are eligible.
No, unless the member obtains prior written pre-approval from the President of the IAI for each webinar.

Yes; verifiable CPD completed through recognised overseas actuarial bodies that are Full Member Associations of the International Actuarial Association (IAA) is fully recognised under APS 9 reciprocity.
Yes, but IFoA CPD hours are discounted by 50% under IAI conversion tables.
explanationCorrect: APS 9 recognises verifiable CPD organized by recognised actuarial bodies (such as IFoA, SOA, CAS, Actuaries Institute Australia) under international reciprocity arrangements.
explanationIncorrect: Reciprocity avoids unnecessary duplication of learning requirements for internationally mobile actuaries.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), CPD Credit as Speaker / Presenter
question: An actuary prepares and delivers a 2-hour technical presentation on Ind AS 117 contractual service margin calculation at the Global Conference of Actuaries. How is their CPD credit calculated?
options: The actuary receives a flat 24 CPD hours, automatically fulfilling their entire annual requirement.
Presenters receive zero CPD credit because teaching others is an unremunerated professional service.
The actuary can only claim credit for the 2 hours of actual speaking time, with zero preparation allowance.
The actuary may claim verifiable CPD credit for both the presentation delivery time and reasonable preparation time, subject to standard daily caps.
explanationCorrect: Under APS 9 guidelines, presenting at recognized professional conferences qualifies for CPD credit covering both actual delivery time and reasonable preparation time, subject to maximum caps.
explanationIncorrect: Preparing high-level technical presentations is recognised as rigorous professional learning.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Technical Research Papers & Publications
question: A Fellow actuary authors a peer-reviewed research paper on climate risk modeling published in an international actuarial journal. Under APS 9, how is this research activity recognised?
options: It does not qualify for any CPD credit unless presented orally at an IAI sessional meeting.
It is classified strictly as 'Other' non-technical learning capped at 3 hours total.
It qualifies as verifiable technical CPD hours in the relevant practice area, subject to Council-approved maximum hour ceilings for published research.
It qualifies only if the paper is co-authored with a sitting Council member.
explanationCorrect: Authoring peer-reviewed actuarial research papers published in recognised journals qualifies as verifiable technical CPD, reflecting deep intellectual contribution.
explanationIncorrect: Research and publication are valued mechanisms for advancing professional knowledge.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Random CPD Audit Sampling
question: Under Section 10.3 of APS 9, how does the Institute verify the veracity of online CPD self-attestations submitted by members?
options: Verification is performed entirely through automated facial recognition during webinars without human sampling.
The Institute does not conduct audits; self-attestations are accepted on trust without verification.
The Institute conducts annual random sample audits requiring selected members to submit physical or electronic proof of attendance and agendas within thirty (30) days.
The Institute audits 100% of all members every six months by conducting on-site workplace inspections.
explanationCorrect: APS 9 establishes random sample audits where selected members must produce supporting attendance records, agendas, and certificates within the stipulated timeframe.
explanationIncorrect: Random audits provide deterrence against fraudulent self-certification while keeping administrative costs manageable.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Pro-Rata CPD for New Fellows Admitted Mid-Year
question: An Associate actuary is admitted to Fellowship and granted a Certificate of Practice on 1st October (exactly halfway through the financial year). What is their CPD obligation for that initial compliance year?
options: They must complete 24 hours plus a retroactive penalty of 6 additional hours.
They are completely exempt from all CPD obligations until the beginning of the next financial year.
They must complete the full 24 verifiable hours regardless of the date of admission.
Their mandatory CPD requirement is calculated on a pro-rata basis for the remaining six months of the compliance year (i.e., 12 verifiable hours).
explanationCorrect: New Fellows admitted mid-year are assigned pro-rated CPD obligations proportionate to the number of full months remaining in the compliance year.
explanationIncorrect: Pro-rating ensures fairness so that new practitioners are not burdened with full-year requirements in a partial year.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Medical & Extended Leave Exemptions
question: A practicing actuary is incapacitated due to major illness and undergoes medical treatment for eight consecutive months during the compliance year. How can they address their CPD shortfall under APS 9?
options: Their Certificate of Practice is automatically revoked with zero possibility of reinstatement.
They are automatically exempt without any notification or paperwork required.
They must arrange for a colleague to attend online webinars under their member account.
They must submit a written application for temporary relief or partial waiver supported by certified medical records to the CPD Committee before the end of the compliance year.
explanationCorrect: Members facing serious medical incapacity, maternity leave, or bereavement can apply for temporary relief or pro-rated waivers with supporting medical documentation.
explanationIncorrect: Formal application and documented evidence ensure legitimate exceptions are handled compassionately and transparently.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), In-House Corporate Actuarial Seminars
question: An insurance company organizes an internal technical workshop on IFRS 17 liability measurement for its actuarial staff. Under what conditions can attendees claim this as verifiable CPD under APS 9?
options: In-house corporate training is strictly ineligible for CPD credit under all circumstances.
Attendees can claim credit only if an external IAI Council member attends as an observer.
Credit is available only if the insurance company pays an accreditation royalty fee to the Institute.
The session must have a predefined formal technical agenda, qualified speakers, verified attendance logs, and a minimum qualifying net duration.
explanationCorrect: In-house technical training qualifies as verifiable CPD provided it has a structured technical agenda, competent presenters, documented attendance records, and satisfies duration thresholds.
explanationIncorrect: Structured corporate learning that meets quality criteria is recognized as valid professional development.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Interactive Webinars & E-Learning Verifiability
question: For an online webinar or asynchronous e-learning module to qualify as 'verifiable' CPD under APS 9, what verification mechanism is mandatory?
options: The member must take a selfie in front of the computer screen and email it to the Executive Director.
Online webinars cannot qualify as verifiable CPD; only physical in-person attendance is accepted.
The member's direct corporate supervisor must sign a statutory affidavit confirming visual observation.
The platform must generate objective proof of participation (e.g., login/logout timestamps, interactive poll responses, or completion assessment certificates).
explanationCorrect: Verifiable CPD requires objective documentation: system-generated attendance logs, time-tracking, poll responses, or completion certificates.
explanationIncorrect: Objective digital verification distinguishes verifiable CPD from unverified informal reading.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Dual Qualification & Overseas CPD Exemption
question: A Fellow of both the IAI and the UK IFoA practices as an Appointed Actuary in India. Can they claim complete exemption from IAI APS 9 on the grounds that they comply with IFoA CPD rules?
options: No, because dual membership automatically cancels practicing rights in India.
Yes; dual qualified Fellows are completely exempt from local Indian CPD compliance under WTO treaties.
No; while IFoA events can be counted towards IAI hours under reciprocity, an actuary holding an IAI Certificate of Practice must fully comply with and report under IAI APS 9 requirements.
Yes, provided they pay an annual overseas reciprocity waiver levy to the Council.
explanationCorrect: Practitioners holding an IAI Certificate of Practice must fulfill IAI APS 9 rules and submit their attestation on the IAI portal, even if qualifying hours were earned through reciprocal bodies.
explanationIncorrect: Local statutory accountability cannot be abdicated to a foreign professional body.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Scope of 'Technical CPD'
question: Under APS 9, which of the following activities falls squarely within the definition of 'Technical CPD' in an actuary's designated practice area?
options: Training on corporate tax deduction at source (TDS) and GST invoice processing.
Advanced stochastic reserving workshops, dynamic financial analysis, climate risk modeling, or IFRS 17 liability valuation.
A corporate human resources seminar on annual employee performance appraisal forms.
General corporate interpersonal negotiation skills and public speaking courses.
explanationCorrect: Technical CPD must directly enhance core actuarial skills: stochastic modeling, reserving, pricing, capital modeling, ALM, or risk quantification.
explanationIncorrect: General business, HR, or non-actuarial tax courses do not qualify as technical actuarial hours.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Cap on 'Other Verifiable Hours'
question: Under APS 9 Section 4.4.3, what is the maximum number of 'Other Verifiable Hours' (such as general leadership, soft skills, or IT tools) that a Category 1 COP holder can count towards their 24 mandatory hours?
options: A maximum of twelve (12) hours per compliance year.
Zero hours; all 24 hours must be technical or professional conduct.
Up to fifteen (15) hours, provided the member passes a computer proficiency test.
A maximum of three (3) hours per compliance year.
explanationCorrect: Section 4.4.3 restricts 'Other' verifiable hours to a strict ceiling of 3 hours out of the 24-hour total, preserving the dominant focus on technical and professional standards.
explanationIncorrect: The 3-hour cap prevents dilution of core technical and ethical competence.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Role of the CPD Committee
question: Which institutional organ is primarily charged with monitoring member compliance, evaluating exceptional waiver requests, and approving accredited CPD events under APS 9?
options: The CPD Committee appointed by the Council of the Institute.
The Quality Review Board acting under Section 43 of the Actuaries Act.
The Appellate Authority constituted by the Central Government.
The Disciplinary Directorate headed by the Director (Discipline).
explanationCorrect: The CPD Committee is the designated functional committee of Council responsible for administering APS 9, reviewing exemptions, and accrediting learning programs.
explanationIncorrect: The CPD Committee manages administrative compliance, referring persistent defaulters to the Disciplinary Directorate.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Fraudulent CPD Self-Attestation
question: An actuary submits an online CPD self-attestation claiming 24 hours of technical attendance, but an audit reveals the attendance certificates were fabricated. Under the Actuaries Act 2006, this is:
options: A minor non-compliance issue that is settled by paying a late fee of Rs. 500.
An administrative error that can be rectified by completing double hours in the following year.
A matter outside the jurisdiction of the Disciplinary Committee.
Grave professional misconduct under the Second Schedule involving moral turpitude and dishonesty, warranting severe disciplinary penalties including potential expulsion.
explanationCorrect: Submitting fabricated CPD certificates is deliberate fraud and moral dishonesty, constituting Second Schedule misconduct subject to suspension or permanent expulsion.
explanationIncorrect: Honesty in professional reporting is a fundamental conduct requirement.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Serving as IAI Examination Marker or Examiner
question: A Fellow actuary serves as an official paper examiner and script marker for Subject SP2 (Life Insurance Specialist Principles). Under APS 9, how is this service recognised?
options: It can only be claimed if the pass rate for the examination paper exceeds 50%.
It does not qualify for any CPD credit because examiners receive financial honoraria from the Institute.
It qualifies strictly as professional conduct CPD capped at 1 hour.
It is recognized as verifiable technical CPD hours in the relevant practice area, subject to Council-approved limits for examination service.
explanationCorrect: Serving as an examiner, question paper setter, or script marker requires deep technical re-examination of syllabus concepts and is recognised as verifiable technical CPD within prescribed caps.
explanationIncorrect: Examination service reinforces core technical mastery in the designated subject.

source: APS 34, Global Pedigree & Adoption Date
question: Which international benchmark does Actuarial Practice Standard 34 (APS 34: General Actuarial Practice) converge with, and when was it officially issued by the IAI Council?
options: It converges directly with International Standard of Actuarial Practice 1 (ISAP 1) issued by the IAA, and was officially issued by IAI on 29 December 2021.
It converges with US GAAP ASC 944 and was officially notified on 1 January 2018.
It converges with International Financial Reporting Standard 4 (IFRS 4) and was adopted in March 2005.
It is an informal advisory guidance note without binding statutory character.
explanationCorrect: APS 34 directly converges with ISAP 1 (General Actuarial Practice) issued by the International Actuarial Association (IAA). Adopted by Council on 4 September 2021, it was officially issued on 29 December 2021.
explanationIncorrect: APS 34 is a formal subordinate statutory standard binding on all Indian actuaries across all practice areas.

source: APS 34, Conflict Hierarchy with Specific Practice Standards
question: Where an apparent conflict arises between general guidance in APS 34 and specific provisions in a practice-area standard (such as APS 2 for Life Insurance or APS 9 for CPD), which standard takes precedence?
options: The conflict must be referred to the High Court for an administrative interpretation before issuing the report.
The specific practice-area standard (e.g., APS 2 or APS 9) strictly takes precedence over the general guidance in APS 34.
APS 34 automatically overrides and supersedes all specific practice standards.
The actuary must apply the most conservative numerical reserve regardless of standard hierarchy.
explanationCorrect: Under the principle of lex specialis derogat legi generali (specific rules override general rules) affirmed in APS 34, standards specific to a particular practice area take precedence over APS 34 in case of conflict.
explanationIncorrect: APS 34 establishes baseline general practice; specialized standards govern domain-specific calculations.

source: APS 34, Section 1.6 (Drafting Conventions: 'Must' vs 'Should')
question: Under Section 1.6 of APS 34, how does the standard legally and operationally distinguish between the terms 'Must' and 'Should'?
options: 'Must' applies only to Appointed Actuaries, while 'Should' applies only to external consulting actuaries.
'Must' indicates an aspirational industry best practice, while 'Should' is mandatory under all circumstances.
'Must' and 'Should' are interchangeable stylistic synonyms carrying identical legal weight under the standard.

'Must' imposes an absolute, unconditional requirement where departure is never permitted unless conflicting with law; 'Should' indicates standard expected practice where departure is permitted only if following it produces inappropriate or misleading results, requiring documentation and disclosure.
explanationCorrect: Section 1.6 defines 'Must' as an absolute obligation (failure to follow = non-compliance unless unlawful), whereas 'Should' establishes a rebuttable presumption (departures require documented justification and report disclosure).
explanationIncorrect: A foundational exam concept: 'Must' is mandatory without exception; 'Should' requires documented rationale and disclosure if departed from.

source: APS 34, Section 1.6 (The Three Gateways to Full Compliance)
question: Under what conditions is an actuary deemed to be in 100% full compliance with APS 34 even when they depart from specific guidance contained in the standard?
options: Departures from APS 34 are never legally permitted under any circumstances.
Whenever the commercial client signs an indemnity waiver releasing the actuary from professional standards.
Whenever following the guidance would cause the insurer to fail statutory solvency margins.

When the departure is compelled by conflicting statutory law, or by a specific practice-area APS, or when departing from a 'should' guidance with documented rationale and report disclosure of the departure and its financial effect.
explanationCorrect: APS 34 establishes three legitimate gateways to compliance: (1) statutory conflict, (2) specific practice standard precedence, or (3) documented and disclosed departure from a 'should' requirement.
explanationIncorrect: Client contracts or commercial convenience can never justify non-compliance with actuarial standards.

source: APS 34, Para 2.1 (Written Terms of Reference)
question: Under APS 34 Para 2.1, what is the mandatory requirement regarding the Terms of Reference (ToR) for an actuarial engagement?
options: The actuary may draft the terms of reference unilaterally and file them confidentially without client confirmation.
Terms of reference are mandatory only for peer reviewers, but optional for lead statutory actuaries.
A verbal understanding between the actuary and the client's finance director is legally sufficient for engagements under Rs. 25 Lakhs.
The actuary must confirm written terms of reference with the principal before starting work, clearly establishing the scope, intended users, role of the actuary, data access, and constraints.
explanationCorrect: Para 2.1 mandates written Terms of Reference prior to starting work, defining scope, intended users, constraints, and deliverables to avoid expectation gaps and misunderstandings.
explanationIncorrect: Written ToR is a vital safeguard that establishes the legal and professional boundaries of the assignment.

source: APS 34, Para 2.3 (Reliance on Others & Disclaimers)
question: An actuary performs an employee gratuity valuation relying entirely on employee demographic records provided by the client's HR department, without performing independent audits of source files. Under APS 34 Para 2.3, what MUST the actuary do in their report?
options: Actuaries are strictly prohibited from relying on third-party or client-provided data under all circumstances.
State in the report that the actuary has independently verified all underlying employee payroll slips.
Omit all references to data sources to prevent client trade secrets from being compromised.
Explicitly disclose the reliance on client-provided data, identify the source, and disclose any limitations or disclaimers of responsibility in the actuarial report.
explanationCorrect: Under Para 2.3 and Section 3.2.2(b), an actuary may rely on information provided by others, but MUST explicitly disclose the reliance, identify the source, and state the extent of any disclaimer of responsibility in the report.
explanationIncorrect: Actuaries frequently rely on client data; full transparency regarding reliance boundaries is legally mandatory.

source: APS 34, Para 2.4 (Materiality Threshold from User Perspective)
question: Under APS 34 Para 2.4, how must an actuary evaluate whether an omission, understatement, or error in an actuarial calculation is 'material'?
options: Materiality is determined solely by the actuary's firm-level professional indemnity deductible limit.
Any mathematical variance exceeding 0.05% of net profit is automatically material.
Materiality must be evaluated strictly from the perspective of the intended users: an item is material if it could reasonably influence the decisions or assessments of intended users.
An error is material only if it exceeds a flat monetary threshold of one crore rupees (Rs. 1,00,00,000).
explanationCorrect: Under Para 2.4, materiality is judged from the perspective of the intended users. If an omission or misstatement could reasonably influence the economic decisions or risk assessments of intended users, it is material.
explanationIncorrect: Materiality is contextual and user-centric, not an arbitrary flat rupee amount.

source: APS 34, Para 2.5 (Data Quality & Reconciliation)
question: An actuary reviewing insurance claims data discovers significant missing date-of-loss fields and evident data corruption in historical accident cohorts. Under APS 34 Para 2.5, how should the actuary proceed?
options: Review data for completeness and consistency, apply appropriate adjustments or proxy assumptions if feasible, and prominently disclose the data deficiencies, adjustments, and resulting limitations in the actuarial report.
Silently remove the corrupted cohort rows from the reserving model without disclosing the modification.
Certify the data as complete and accurate to avoid delays in financial reporting deadlines.
Proceed with the valuation using corrupted data while obtaining a signed liability waiver from the chief claims manager.
explanationCorrect: Under Para 2.5 and Section 3.2.2(d), actuaries must review data quality. If adjustments or proxy assumptions are applied, the deficiencies, adjustments, and their impact on uncertainty must be disclosed in the report.
explanationIncorrect: Silent deletion or false certifications of corrupted data constitute gross professional negligence.

source: APS 34, Paras 2.6 - 2.8 (Assumption Setting & Reasonableness in Aggregate)
question: When setting actuarial assumptions for liability valuation, what dual standard must an actuary satisfy under APS 34 Para 2.7?
options: Each assumption must be individually justifiable AND the assumptions must be reasonable in the aggregate, ensuring that multiple conservative margins do not compound into an absurd distortion.
Assumptions only need to be justifiable in the aggregate; individual assumptions may be arbitrary or contradictory.
Assumptions must be set strictly by the client's finance director, with the actuary serving only as a calculating agent.
Every individual assumption must be calibrated to the 99.5th percentile worst-case historical scenario.
explanationCorrect: Under Para 2.7, assumptions set by the actuary must be justifiable individually AND reasonable in the aggregate. Compounding multiple conservative margins can distort financial reality and mislead users.
explanationIncorrect: Both individual reasonableness and aggregate coherence are mandatory under APS 34.

source: APS 34, Para 2.8 (Client-Prescribed Assumptions)
question: A corporate pension client instructs an actuary to adopt a 12% annual salary inflation assumption that the actuary considers unrealistically low compared to recent historical trends. Under APS 34 Para 2.8, how must the actuary handle this prescribed assumption?
options: The actuary must alter historical demographic records to artificially force the 12% assumption to fit the model.
The actuary must disclose in the report that the assumption was prescribed by the client, identify who prescribed it, disclose their stated rationale, and explain the financial impact on results.
The actuary must refuse to issue any actuarial report and resign from the engagement immediately.
The actuary must silently adopt the assumption as their own professional estimate to preserve client relationship.
explanationCorrect: Under Para 2.8 and Section 3.2.2(g), where an assumption is prescribed by the principal that the actuary cannot professionally support, the actuary must disclose who prescribed it, their rationale, and the financial impact on the valuation results.
explanationIncorrect: Transparency protects intended users from assuming the prescribed figure represents the actuary's independent expert judgment.

source: APS 34, Para 2.10 (Model Governance: Independent Validation)
question: Under APS 34 Para 2.10, what is the mandatory structural governance control required for complex financial and reserving models?
options: Change control logs are required only when models are deployed in cloud computing environments.
The model developer may validate their own spreadsheets provided they sign a self-certification statement.
Model validation and testing must be performed by individuals who are independent of model development, with formal change control procedures that log all modifications and allow reversal.
Model validation is mandatory only if the model is coded in an open-source programming language.
explanationCorrect: Para 2.10 mandates rigorous model governance: model validation must be conducted by individuals independent of model development, with documented change control preventing unauthorized edits and logging all changes.
explanationIncorrect: Self-validation by model developers creates self-review bias and violates model governance standards.

source: APS 34, Para 2.13 (Subsequent Events Handling)
question: Between the balance sheet valuation date (31 March) and the report signing date (15 May), a severe earthquake causes catastrophic property damage to an insurer's insured portfolio. Under APS 34 Para 2.13, how must the actuary treat this subsequent event?
options: Back-date the actuarial valuation signature to 30 March to avoid regulatory disclosure requirements.
Evaluate whether the subsequent event materially alters financial reality, and disclose the nature of the event and an estimate of its financial effect in the report.
Adjust the 31 March balance sheet reserves directly without disclosing that the event occurred in May.
Disregard the event completely because it occurred outside the financial accounting reporting year.
explanationCorrect: Under Para 2.13 and Section 3.2.2(k), material subsequent events occurring between the calculation date and report release date that would influence intended users must be disclosed with estimated financial effects.
explanationIncorrect: Ignoring material post-balance-sheet catastrophes misleads intended users on solvency.

source: APS 34, Para 2.14 (The Peer Replicability Documentation Test)
question: What is the statutory and professional benchmark mandated by APS 34 Para 2.14 for determining whether actuarial documentation is legally sufficient?
options: Only the original certifying actuary needs to be able to decipher the model logic and parameter inputs.
The documentation is sufficient if it contains at least one hundred pages of mathematical appendices.
The documentation is sufficient if the corporate client confirms written satisfaction with the final valuation figure.

The documentation is sufficient ONLY IF another actuary qualified in the same practice area can review the files, understand the methodology, replicate the calculations, and evaluate the reasonableness of all professional judgments.
explanationCorrect: Para 2.14 establishes the famous 'Peer Replicability Test': working papers and models must be documented to a standard where another qualified actuary in the same field could replicate calculations and evaluate professional judgments.
explanationIncorrect: A cornerstone concept of actuarial professionalism: personal idiosyncratic working files that no other actuary can replicate fail the statutory documentation test.

source: APS 34, Section 3.2.2 (The 11 Mandatory Report Disclosures)
question: Under Section 3.2.2 of APS 34, how many specific mandatory disclosure categories are prescribed to be included in an actuarial report whenever applicable?
options: Exactly five (5) disclosures covering date, client name, actuary name, fee amount, and final reserve.
Twenty-four (24) disclosures corresponding to the twenty-four sections of the Insurance Act 1938.
Mandatory disclosures are not enumerated in APS 34; disclosure content is left entirely to individual discretion.
Exactly eleven (11) mandatory disclosure categories (items a through k), covering deviations, reliance on others, data adjustments, prescribed assumptions, model limitations, and subsequent events.
explanationCorrect: Section 3.2.2 lists exactly 11 distinct disclosure categories (a through k) that an actuarial report must address whenever applicable to provide full transparency to intended users.
explanationIncorrect: These 11 disclosures ensure intended users understand constraints, reliances, departures, and data limitations.

source: APS 34, Section 3.1 (Communication to Intended Users)
question: Under APS 34 Section 3.1, who are considered the 'intended users' of an actuarial communication or report?
options: Exclusively the statutory financial auditor appointed under the Companies Act 2013.
Any third-party investor who obtains an unauthorized leaked copy of the report through financial news media.
The principal (client/employer) and any other party whom the actuary identified in the Terms of Reference or report as a legitimate user of the actuarial findings.
Any competitor insurance company operating in the same domestic market segment.
explanationCorrect: Section 3.1 defines intended users as the principal and any other parties specifically recognized by the actuary in the terms of reference or report as intended recipients of the actuarial findings.
explanationIncorrect: Actuaries owe professional duty of care to intended users, not to unforeseen third parties relying on unauthorized leaked drafts.

source: APS 34, Section 3.1.2 (Unintended Users & Distribution Restrictions)
question: To prevent unintended third parties from inappropriately relying on specialized actuarial findings, what operational control should an actuary implement under APS 34?
options: Refuse to provide a written report and deliver all valuation results exclusively through verbal phone calls.

Include an explicit distribution limitation and user restriction clause in the report stating that the report is prepared solely for the principal and intended users, disclaiming liability to third parties.
File a copyright patent application for the valuation report with the Indian Patent Office.
Require the client to pay an indemnity deposit of Rs. 10 Lakhs before releasing the report.
explanationCorrect: Section 3.1.2 advises actuaries to include clear distribution limitation statements and disclaimers of liability to unintended users, preventing inappropriate external reliance.
explanationIncorrect: Distribution clauses define the legal boundaries of duty of care to prevent third-party liability.

source: APS 34, Para 2.2 (Selection of Actuarial Methodology)
question: Under APS 34 Para 2.2, when selecting an actuarial method or model for a specific engagement, what criteria should the actuary consider?
options: The actuary should select the methodology that produces the lowest statutory liability for the insurer.
The methodology must be appropriate to the purpose, proportional to the nature and complexity of the underlying risks, and compatible with the quality and granularity of available data.
The methodology must be chosen by a majority vote of the client's board of directors.
The actuary must always select the most mathematically complex stochastic algorithm available in the literature.
explanationCorrect: Para 2.2 emphasizes proportionality and fitness for purpose: methods must fit the nature of the engagement, the materiality of risks, and the characteristics of available data.
explanationIncorrect: Methodology selection is an actuarial responsibility governed by suitability, data availability, and proportionality.

source: APS 34, Para 2.11 (Sensitivity and Scenario Analysis)
question: Why does APS 34 Para 2.11 emphasize the performance of sensitivity testing and scenario analysis in actuarial work?
options: To eliminate all financial and economic uncertainty from the valuation balance sheet.
To enable the client to select the most commercially convenient valuation reserve figure from a menu of options.
To understand and communicate the sensitivity of results to key assumptions and parameter variations, highlighting the degree of inherent uncertainty to intended users.
To fulfill a mechanical procedural checklist that has no bearing on professional opinions.
explanationCorrect: Para 2.11 highlights that actuarial estimates involve uncertainty; sensitivity analysis identifies key drivers of risk and helps intended users comprehend the potential variability of future outcomes.
explanationIncorrect: Sensitivity testing is an essential communication tool for illustrating uncertainty.

source: APS 34, Para 2.9 (Internal Consistency of Assumptions)
question: When setting financial assumptions involving discount rates, salary growth, inflation, and investment returns, what requirement does APS 34 Para 2.9 impose?
options: The actuary must assume zero inflation if salary growth assumptions are positive.
Financial assumptions must remain completely static across ten consecutive financial years.
The economic assumptions must be internally consistent with one another and reflect coherent macroeconomic relationships (e.g., real discount rate vs inflation).
Each financial assumption must be calibrated completely independently using unrelated macroeconomic datasets.
explanationCorrect: Para 2.9 requires internal consistency among assumptions: economic variables (discount rates, price inflation, wage growth, investment returns) must reflect coherent economic linkages.
explanationIncorrect: Internally inconsistent assumptions (e.g. 10% inflation with a 4% nominal discount rate) produce illogical and distorted liability calculations.

source: APS 34, Section 3.2.1 (Clarity of Actuarial Reports)
question: Under APS 34 Section 3.2.1, what core standard must an actuary uphold regarding the style and language of an actuarial communication?
options: The report should omit technical appendices to keep total length under five pages.
The communication must be clear, comprehensible, and organized in a manner that enables intended users to understand the implications of the results and the risks involved.
The language must be drafted exclusively in archaic legal phrasing to minimize professional liability.
The report must use dense mathematical notation to demonstrate intellectual rigor to non-technical readers.
explanationCorrect: Section 3.2.1 emphasizes that reports must be clear, well-structured, and intelligible to their intended audience, bridging the technical gap so users can make informed decisions.
explanationIncorrect: Obscure or impenetrable drafting fails the professional communication standard.

source: APS 34, Para 2.12 (Peer Review / Independent Review)
question: Under APS 34 Para 2.12, what is the role and importance of an independent peer review before an actuarial work product is finalized?
options: The peer reviewer assumes 100% of the legal liability for the report, releasing the lead actuary from statutory responsibility.
Peer review is mandatory only if the lead actuary has less than two years of post-qualification experience.
Peer review is a commercial marketing tool used solely to justify premium billing rates to clients.
An independent peer review provides objective technical scrutiny of data, methodologies, assumptions, and reporting, reducing the risk of material error and bias.
explanationCorrect: Para 2.12 underscores peer review as a vital quality assurance control: an independent qualified review helps identify errors, challenge assumptions, and ensure compliance with standards.
explanationIncorrect: Peer review enhances report credibility and mitigates individual modeling blind spots.

source: APS 34, Section 3.2.2(a) (Conflict of Interest Disclosure)
question: An actuary prepares a statutory valuation report for a firm where the actuary's spouse serves as Chief Financial Officer. Under APS 34 Section 3.2.2(a), what MUST be disclosed in the report?
options: The actuary must clearly disclose any conflict of interest, personal relationship, or financial interest that could impair, or be perceived to impair, their professional objectivity.
The conflict disclosure can be omitted if the valuation result is reviewed by an actuarial analyst.
The actuary is prohibited from mentioning family relationships to protect personal privacy.
The actuary must disclose the conflict only if the spouse's equity holdings exceed 50% of the company.
explanationCorrect: Section 3.2.2(a) requires transparent disclosure of any actual or potential conflicts of interest in the report so intended users can assess the objectivity of the actuarial advice.
explanationIncorrect: Concealing material conflicts of interest in valuation reports violates both APS 34 and the PCS.

source: APS 34, Section 3.2.2(i) (Disclosure of Statutory Departures)
question: Where an actuary is forced to depart from a specific provision of APS 34 because it conflicts with a mandatory IRDAI regulation, what is the reporting requirement under Section 3.2.2(i)?
options: The actuary must disclose the specific standard departed from, cite the conflicting statutory provision, explain the rationale, and quantify or explain the financial effect of the departure.
The actuary must issue an adverse opinion declaring the insurance company's financial statements invalid.
The actuary must silently obey the IRDAI regulation without mentioning APS 34 in the report.
The actuary must obtain a written exemption certificate from the President of the Institute before signing.
explanationCorrect: Section 3.2.2(i) requires full transparency when statutory law overrides standards: the report must disclose the departure, the governing law, and the impact on the actuarial results.
explanationIncorrect: Law prevails over professional standards, but the departure must be documented and disclosed.

source: APS 34, Para 2.10 (Vendor Software & Third-Party Models)
question: An actuarial team utilizes a commercial proprietary black-box software package for capital modeling. Under APS 34 Para 2.10, what is the actuary's professional obligation?
options: The actuary is completely absolved of all modeling errors because liability rests exclusively with the commercial software vendor.
The actuary remains responsible for the work product and must satisfy themselves that the software is appropriate, understand its underlying methodology and limitations, and validate its outputs.
The actuary must decompile and rewrite the vendor's source code in Python before running calculations.
Actuaries are forbidden from using third-party commercial software for statutory reporting.
explanationCorrect: Para 2.10 makes clear that using external vendor models does not delegate professional responsibility: the actuary must understand the model's logic, parameters, limitations, and validate its fitness.
explanationIncorrect: Blind reliance on 'black-box' vendor models fails professional due diligence requirements.

source: APS 34, Section 3.1.3 (Draft vs Final Actuarial Communications)
question: An actuary shares an interim preliminary spreadsheet with a client's finance team marked 'DRAFT - For Discussion Only'. Under APS 34, how should preliminary communications be governed?
options: Preliminary drafts are exempt from all professional standards and can contain arbitrary figures.
The actuary should clearly identify preliminary or draft communications, state that they are subject to change, and caution intended users against relying on them for final financial decisions.
Actuaries are strictly prohibited from sharing draft findings with clients prior to final report signing.
Draft communications are legally binding contracts that cannot be amended in the final report.
explanationCorrect: Preliminary communications must be clearly flagged as drafts with explicit caveats warning against premature reliance, preventing misunderstandings before final validation.
explanationIncorrect: Draft labeling protects both the client and the practitioner during iterative analysis.

source: APS 34, Co-Signing Actuaries & Shared Liability
question: Two qualified actuaries jointly sign a statutory valuation report. Under professional standards and APS 34, how is professional responsibility shared between them?
options: Only the actuary who drafted the mathematical spreadsheets bears liability; the second signature is purely ceremonial.
The senior partner bears 100% of the liability while the junior partner is completely exempt.
Co-signing an actuarial report is prohibited under the Actuaries Act 2006.
Both actuaries share joint and several professional responsibility for the entire report, unless the report explicitly defines a clear division of responsibility between them.
explanationCorrect: Co-signatories share full professional responsibility for the entire actuarial communication unless a specific, documented division of scope is disclosed in the report.
explanationIncorrect: Signing an actuarial report carries personal professional accountability that cannot be treated as ceremonial.

source: APS 34, Discovery of Material Errors Post-Issuance
question: Three weeks after releasing a final actuarial report, the actuary discovers a coding error that overstated the client's asset-liability surplus by Rs. 50 Crores. Under APS 34 and professional ethics, what MUST the actuary do?
options: Resign immediately from the Institute to avoid disciplinary investigation.
Destroy all working spreadsheets and claim that the client provided erroneous data.
Conceal the error until the following financial year's annual valuation cycle.
Promptly notify the principal and intended users of the error, explain its nature and financial impact, and issue a revised or corrected communication as appropriate.
explanationCorrect: When a material error is discovered post-release, professional integrity requires immediate notification to intended users and issuance of corrected results to prevent misinformed decisions.
explanationIncorrect: Prompt correction and disclosure uphold public trust; concealment constitutes grave professional misconduct.

source: APS 34, Executive Summaries & Balanced Presentation
question: When an actuarial report includes an executive summary for corporate board members, what requirement does APS 34 impose regarding its balance?
options: The executive summary should present only optimistic conclusions to avoid alarming the board.
The executive summary may omit all references to uncertainty if the final reserve is within statutory limits.
Executive summaries are legally prohibited in actuarial reports to force readers to read all technical appendices.
The executive summary must fairly and accurately reflect the findings of the main report, including material caveats, uncertainties, and limitations, without being selectively biased.
explanationCorrect: Executive summaries must be balanced and fair, conveying critical caveats and uncertainties alongside key figures so decision-makers receive a true, unvarnished picture.
explanationIncorrect: Selective cherry-picking in executive summaries misleads non-technical board members.

source: APS 34, Archiving & Version Control of Working Files
question: Under the model governance and documentation provisions of APS 34, what must an actuary ensure regarding the archiving of model versions and datasets used for final reports?
options: Working files only need to be preserved if the client pays an archiving fee.
Model files can be overwritten as soon as newer monthly updates are processed.
Archiving is required only for models built in mainframe COBOL software.
The exact versions of data files, model code, parameter settings, and run logs used to produce the final report must be archived and protected against overwriting to ensure replicability.
explanationCorrect: To satisfy the peer replicability test (Para 2.14), the exact data snapshot, model version, and configuration used for the signed report must be securely archived.
explanationIncorrect: Overwriting working models destroys the evidentiary trail required for peer review and statutory audit.

source: APS 34, Expressing an Actuarial Opinion vs Factual Summary
question: How must an actuary distinguish between factual data and professional opinions within an actuarial report under APS 34?
options: Actuaries are legally prohibited from expressing opinions on future financial events.

The report must clearly distinguish between factual statements (e.g. historical claims paid) and actuarial opinions, assumptions, or projections, indicating where professional judgment has been applied.
Factual data and actuarial projections must be blended seamlessly so users cannot differentiate them.
Actuarial reports must contain only mathematical formulas without any narrative interpretation.
explanationCorrect: Clear reporting requires distinguishing objective historical facts from subjective assumptions, models, and professional estimates so users understand the degree of judgment involved.
explanationIncorrect: Confusing historical facts with prospective estimates obscures the boundaries of uncertainty.

source: FT-IGN 31, Section 1.2 & ICAI SA 620 (Auditor's Expert Role)
question: Under FT-IGN 31 and ICAI Standard on Auditing SA 620, what is the precise statutory and legal role of an Auditing Actuary supporting an insurer's statutory financial audit?
options: The Auditing Actuary is an internal compliance officer employed by the audited insurer's risk committee.
The Auditing Actuary operates as an 'Auditor's Expert' assisting the statutory financial auditor; the statutory financial auditor retains sole legal responsibility for the overall audit opinion.
The Auditing Actuary serves as an independent technical arbitrator whose determinations are legally binding on both the auditor and the regulator.
The Auditing Actuary replaces the statutory financial auditor and signs the primary audit opinion jointly with the company secretary.
explanationCorrect: Under FT-IGN 31 and ICAI SA 620, the Auditing Actuary serves as an Auditor's Expert. The statutory financial auditor relies on the actuary's technical findings, but retains sole legal responsibility for the audit opinion.
explanationIncorrect: The actuary does not sign the audit report itself; they provide technical challenge, review, and assurance to the financial audit team.

source: FT-IGN 31, Section 3.2.4 (Pre-Engagement 1-Year Cooling-Off Period)
question: Actuary R is invited to serve as the Auditing Actuary for an insurance company. Within the preceding 9 months, Actuary R had served as the company's external consulting actuary advising on pricing and reserving models. Can Actuary R accept the role under FT-IGN 31 Section 3.2.4?
options: Yes, because prior consulting knowledge enables a more comprehensive and efficient audit inspection.
Yes, provided Actuary R establishes an internal ethical firewall within their consulting firm.
Yes, provided the Board Audit Committee issues a formal resolution approving the appointment.
No; FT-IGN 31 mandates a strict pre-engagement cooling-off period of at least one year (1 year) if the actuary has provided valuation consulting or served as an employee/AA to the insurer.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 3.2.4, an actuary cannot accept an Auditing Actuary appointment if within the preceding 1 year they were an employee, Appointed Actuary, or provided reserving/pricing consulting, due to the severe self-review threat.
explanationIncorrect: Auditing one's own previous work violates the core principle of auditor independence under ICAI and IAI standards.

source: FT-IGN 31, Section 3.2.5 (Partner Rotation & Cooling-Off Timeline)
question: Under FT-IGN 31 Section 3.2.5, what is the maximum continuous tenure for which an individual Auditing Actuary may serve for a specific insurance company, and what cooling-off period applies?
options: Tenure is unlimited provided the actuary undergoes an annual external peer review.
Maximum tenure of seven (7) consecutive years, with no mandatory cooling-off period.
Maximum tenure of four (4) consecutive financial years, followed by a mandatory cooling-off period of at least three (3) consecutive years.
Maximum tenure of five (5) consecutive financial years, followed by a mandatory cooling-off period of one (1) year.
explanationCorrect: Section 3.2.5 establishes the rotation safeguard to mitigate familiarity threats: maximum continuous tenure of 4 consecutive years, followed by a mandatory 3-year cooling-off period before reappointment.
explanationIncorrect: The 4-year tenure and 3-year cooling-off safeguard maintains ongoing fresh, objective challenge in statutory insurance audits.

source: FT-IGN 31, Section 3.2.5 (Concurrent Engagement Ceiling)
question: Under FT-IGN 31 Section 3.2.5, what is the maximum number of insurance or reinsurance companies for which an individual Auditing Actuary may serve as the lead signing actuary concurrently?
options: Not more than five (5) insurance companies concurrently.
There is no statutory cap; actuaries may accept unlimited appointments subject to firm capacity.
Not more than three (3) insurance or reinsurance companies concurrently.
Not more than seven (7) companies, aligning with statutory auditor limits under the Companies Act 2013.
explanationCorrect: Section 3.2.5 caps concurrent engagements at a maximum of 3 insurance or reinsurance companies to prevent over-extension and ensure adequate partner time and scrutiny.
explanationIncorrect: Auditing statutory insurance liabilities under Ind AS 117 is highly complex and time-intensive, justifying the 3-company cap.

source: FT-IGN 31, Section 3.19.5 (Working Paper Access Asymmetry)
question: During an Ind AS 117 statutory audit, the Chief Financial Officer (CFO) of the audited insurer demands full copies of the Auditing Actuary's internal challenge memos and private models. Under FT-IGN 31 Section 3.19.5, how is this demand treated?
options: Insurer management has RESTRICTED ACCESS and has no statutory right to inspect internal challenge memos, audit working papers, or confidential communications between the Auditing Actuary and the statutory auditor.
Working papers are joint intellectual property and must be accessible to both the insurer and the auditor.
The CFO has an unconditional statutory right to inspect all audit working papers under corporate disclosure laws.
The Auditing Actuary must provide working papers provided the CFO signs a non-disclosure agreement.
explanationCorrect: Section 3.19.5 establishes the principle of Working Paper Access Asymmetry: the statutory auditor has full unfettered access, while insurer management has restricted access to preserve audit independence and prevent management interference.
explanationIncorrect: A heavily tested exam concept: Management cannot demand to inspect the auditor's internal challenge memoranda.

source: FT-IGN 31, Section 3.23 (Five-Stage Dispute Escalation Protocol)
question: When an unresolved material disagreement arises between the Auditing Actuary and the Appointed Actuary regarding liability valuation under Ind AS 117, what is the formal 5-stage escalation pathway under FT-IGN 31?
options: Level 1: Working Level (Auditing Actuary & AA) -> Level 2: Audit Partner Level -> Level 3: Governance Review (EQCR & Audit Committee) -> Level 4: Board of Directors / TCWG -> Level 5: Statutory Regulators (IRDAI & IAI Disciplinary Directorate).
Level 1: Appointed Actuary -> Level 2: Chief Risk Officer -> Level 3: High Court -> Level 4: Central Government -> Level 5: International Actuarial Association.
Level 1: Audit Committee -> Level 2: Statutory Auditor -> Level 3: Ministry of Finance -> Level 4: IRDAI -> Level 5: Civil Court.
Level 1: Informal Discussion -> Level 2: Commercial Arbitration -> Level 3: Judicial Mediation -> Level 4: Public Disclose -> Level 5: Immediate Resignation.
explanationCorrect: Section 3.23 provides a structured 5-stage escalation pathway moving systematically from technical working dialogue up through audit partners, board audit committee, full board, and ultimately statutory regulators.
explanationIncorrect: The 5-stage protocol ensures systematic governance challenge before invoking regulatory whistleblowing.

source: FT-IGN 31, Section 3.23.6 (Level 5 Escalation: Public Interest Confidentiality Override)
question: At Level 5 of the disagreement escalation pathway under FT-IGN 31 Section 3.23.6, the Auditing Actuary reports unrectified material misstatements to IRDAI and the IAI. Does this disclosure breach client confidentiality under PCS v4.0?
options: No; client confidentiality is legally overridden in the public interest and under statutory regulatory reporting obligations at Level 5.
No, but only if the disclosure is made anonymously through a sealed letter.
Yes; reporting to regulators without prior board clearance is an actionable breach of client confidentiality under PCS v4.0.
Yes, unless the Auditing Actuary obtains an advance court injunction protecting them from civil damages.
explanationCorrect: Under FT-IGN 31 Section 3.23.6 and PCS v4.0 Para 3.2, reporting to statutory regulators at Level 5 to prevent material financial misstatement operates under the public interest and statutory reporting exceptions, overriding confidentiality.
explanationIncorrect: Public interest and regulator reporting obligations strictly supersede client confidentiality at Level 5 escalation.

source: FT-IGN 31, Section 3.10.2A & Ind AS 117 (PAA Eligibility Safe Harbour)
question: An insurer writing a 3-year multi-year health insurance policy attempts to qualify for the simplified Premium Allocation Approach (PAA) under Ind AS 117 by arguing that the policy is re-underwritten annually, treating it as three 1-year tranches. How does FT-IGN 31 Section 3.10.2A evaluate this?
options: It is acceptable provided the insurer's Appointed Actuary issues a certification of mathematical equivalence.
It is fully compliant provided the insurer tracks unearned premium separately for each twelve-month period.

It is strictly non-compliant; PAA safe harbour under Para 53(b) requires the coverage period of the whole contract to be 1 year or less; artificially subdividing multi-year contracts without substantive contract boundary termination is prohibited.
It is permitted only if the policyholder retains an unconditional cancellation right with full refund.
explanationCorrect: Under FT-IGN 31 Section 3.10.2A and Ind AS 117, the PAA 1-year safe harbour applies strictly at the whole-contract level; insurers cannot artificially slice multi-year policies into 1-year tranches unless a substantive contract boundary exists under Para 34.
explanationIncorrect: Manufacturing PAA eligibility by slicing multi-year contracts is an explicit audit fraud risk highlighted in FT-IGN 31.

source: FT-IGN 31, Section 3.14.2 & IRDAI Directives (Prescribed Discount Curve)
question: Under FT-IGN 31 Section 3.14.2 and IRDAI directives, which discount curve must strictly be utilized to discount liability cash flows under Ind AS 117 in India?
options: The State Bank of India Marginal Cost of Funds Based Lending Rate (MCLR).
The Reserve Bank of India 91-day Treasury Bill rate compounded semi-annually.
The London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR) transition benchmark.
The Clearing Corporation of India Limited (CCIL) Zero-Coupon Yield Curve.
explanationCorrect: FT-IGN 31 Section 3.14.2 confirms that IRDAI mandates the use of the CCIL (Clearing Corporation of India Limited) Zero-Coupon Yield Curve as the official risk-free benchmark for Ind AS 117 discounting.
explanationIncorrect: Using unverified internal rates or foreign curves breaches statutory Indian accounting and actuarial standards.

source: FT-IGN 31, Section 3.13 (Risk Adjustment for Non-Financial Risk)
question: Under Ind AS 117 and FT-IGN 31 Section 3.13, how is the Risk Adjustment for Non-Financial Risk (RA) conceptually defined and disclosed?
options: It is an arbitrary contingency margin fixed at exactly 10% of present value of future claims.

It reflects the compensation an entity requires for bearing the uncertainty about the amount and timing of cash flows, measured from the entity's perspective, with mandatory disclosure of the equivalent confidence level (percentile) under Para 119.
It represents a regulatory capital buffer maintained in escrow with the central bank.
It reflects the market-wide systemic risk premium traded on public stock exchanges, disclosed as an equity beta.
explanationCorrect: Risk Adjustment (RA) under Ind AS 117 reflects entity-specific compensation for bearing non-financial risk. Para 119 strictly mandates disclosure of the equivalent confidence level percentile if non-VaR techniques (e.g. Cost of Capital) are used.
explanationIncorrect: The equivalent percentile disclosure under Para 119 is a key focus of the Auditing Actuary's technical review.

source: FT-IGN 31, Section 3.11.4 (Post-Model Adjustments Threshold)
question: Under FT-IGN 31 Section 3.11.4, when do Post-Model Adjustments (PMAs) or manual management overlays trigger mandatory deep technical audit challenge by the Auditing Actuary?
options: PMAs trigger audit challenge only if they remain unreversed for more than three reporting cycles.
When PMAs exceed 10% of total company gross written premium.
When PMAs alter the net underwriting profit by more than Rs. 50 Lakhs.
When manual PMAs exceed 5% of Contractual Service Margin (CSM) or 2% of the Liability for Remaining Coverage (LRC).
explanationCorrect: Section 3.11.4 identifies PMAs exceeding 5% of CSM or 2% of LRC as material risk indicators requiring exhaustive verification of empirical justification, governance approvals, and reversal tracking.
explanationIncorrect: Unjustified manual overlays can be used to manipulate profit emergence; hence the strict 5% CSM / 2% LRC threshold.

source: FT-IGN 31, Section 3.19.4 & SA 230 (Audit Working Paper Retention)
question: Under FT-IGN 31 Section 3.19.4 and ICAI Standard on Auditing SA 230, for what minimum period must the Auditing Actuary retain all audit working papers, challenge memos, and valuation models?
options: Exactly five years (5 years) matching the general APS 9 CPD document retention rule.
Ten years (10 years) under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act guidelines.
Three years (3 years) aligning with the general commercial dispute limitation under Indian law.
A minimum period of seven years (7 years) from the date of the auditor's report.
explanationCorrect: Under FT-IGN 31 Section 3.19.4 and ICAI SA 230 ('Audit Documentation'), the Auditing Actuary's working papers and audit challenge records must be preserved for at least seven years (7 years) from the date of the audit report.
explanationIncorrect: CRITICAL DISTINCTION: CPD records must be retained for 5 years (APS 9), while statutory audit documentation must be preserved for 7 years (ICAI SA 230 / FT-IGN 31).

source: FT-IGN 31, Section 3.2.3 & SA 220 (Engagement Quality Control Reviewer - EQCR)
question: Under FT-IGN 31 Section 3.2.3 and ICAI SA 220, what is the role and requirement of an Engagement Quality Control Reviewer (EQCR) for high-risk insurance audits?
options: A retrospective quality inspection performed twelve months after the publication of audited accounts.
A review of client billing rates and engagement profitability performed by the firm's managing partner.
A mandatory independent partner review of significant professional judgments, models, and conclusions conducted prior to the issuance of the actuarial audit report.
An external audit evaluation conducted by the Institute's Disciplinary Directorate.
explanationCorrect: Under SA 220 and FT-IGN 31, an EQCR is an independent partner who objectively evaluates the significant judgments and conclusions of the engagement team before the audit opinion is signed.
explanationIncorrect: EQCR hot reviews ensure robust second-pair-of-eyes scrutiny on high-stakes public interest entities.

source: FT-IGN 31, Ind AS 117 Treatment of Onerous Contracts (Loss Component)
question: Under Ind AS 117 and FT-IGN 31, how must an insurer account for a group of insurance contracts that is determined to be onerous (loss-making) at initial recognition?
options: Defer the day-one loss as an asset and amortize it systematically over the policy term.
Recognize the net loss immediately in profit or loss, establishing a Loss Component within the Liability for Remaining Coverage (LRC); the loss CANNOT be deferred against future CSM.
Recognize the loss in Other Comprehensive Income (OCI) to avoid distorting operating underwriting results.
Offset the loss against profitable groups within the same broad insurance portfolio.
explanationCorrect: Under Ind AS 117, onerous contracts do not have a CSM; the day-one loss must be recognized immediately in profit or loss, tracking the loss component within the LRC.
explanationIncorrect: Earnings smoothing or deferral of day-one losses is strictly prohibited under Ind AS 117.

source: FT-IGN 31, Section 3.19.2 (Cold Quality Reviews under SQC 1)
question: What is the distinction between a 'Hot Review' (SA 220) and a 'Cold Review' (SQC 1) in the quality control framework governing an Auditing Actuary firm?
options: A Hot Review (EQCR) is conducted before the audit report is signed to catch errors in real time; a Cold Review is an inspection of completed audit files conducted by independent partners after report issuance to evaluate firm-wide adherence to standards.
A Hot Review is conducted by external regulators while a Cold Review is performed by internal staff.
A Hot Review covers life insurance portfolios while a Cold Review covers non-life property and casualty portfolios.
A Hot Review evaluates financial calculations while a Cold Review evaluates word formatting and grammar.
explanationCorrect: Under SQC 1 and SA 220, Hot Reviews (EQCR) occur pre-issuance to ensure report integrity; Cold Reviews occur post-issuance as part of ongoing internal monitoring of audit methodology and compliance.
explanationIncorrect: Both hot and cold reviews form the dual pillars of audit quality control in actuarial audit practice.

source: FT-IGN 31, Ind AS 117 Measurement Models: GMM as Default
question: Under Ind AS 117, which measurement approach serves as the mandatory default model for all insurance contracts unless specific qualifying criteria for alternative approaches are met?
